p.seg: What the sages and worthies praise,
nothing is more praised than intelligence;
(Heaven manifests its image through the three lights,
humans demonstrate their measure through intelligence.)
What is most valued in intelligence,
is nothing more valued than understanding people.
(Being adept in writing and arithmetic
is one art among the six arts;
being discerning about character and talent
is the overall responsibility of official selection.)
If understanding people with genuine wisdom is achieved,
then all talents can be properly ordered,
and the endeavors of various achievements will flourish.
Therefore, when the sages composed the hexagrams and images,
they established the distinctions between the noble person and the petty person.
(The noble person is the teacher of the petty person,
the petty person is the resource for the noble person,
teacher and resource complement each other,
this has long been the case.)
When arranging the Odes and recording aspirations,
they differentiated the tasks of customs, elegance, and correctness;
(The nine regions have different customs,
the five directions have varied practices,
thus the sages established their teachings without changing local ways,
instituted their governance without altering local customs.)
When instituting rituals and music,
they examined the virtues of reverence and constancy in the six arts;
(Although not changing their methods,
they always prioritized poetry and rituals;
although not altering customs,
they always based them on filial piety and fraternal duty.)
Personally facing south as ruler,
they recruited outstanding and辅助 talents.
All these are means to promote various excellences and accomplish heavenly achievements.
(Continuing heaven's work and completing things,
their responsibility is extremely heavy.
Thus seeking the worthy and recommending the good,
they always acted as if never sufficient.)
Once heavenly achievements are accomplished,
then all receive fame and praise.
(Loyal ministers exhaust their strength to contribute effectiveness,
enlightened rulers obtain worthies and rest easy,
superiors and inferiors are loyal and loving,
how could slander and criticism arise?)
Thus Yáo was praised for being able to illuminate outstanding virtue,
Shùn achieved merit by promoting the Eight Worthies and Eight Kind Ones;
Tāng gained fame by selecting the worthy from Yǒushēn,
King Wén was honored for elevating the old man from the Wèi riverbank.
From this we can discuss:
when sages promote virtue,
who does not labor with intelligence in seeking people,
gaining ease by appointing capable agents?
(Gathering scholars and feeding oxen,
this is how Duke Mù of Qín dominated the Western Rong;
addressing one as "Father Zhong",
this is how Duke Huán of Qí achieved nine assemblies of lords.)
Therefore, though Confucius was not tested in office,
and had no means of promotion,
he still categorized his disciples into four disciplines,
and broadly discussed various talents to distinguish three grades.
(Promoting virtuous conduct as the foremost of the four disciplines,
describing innate knowledge as the highest of the three grades;
illuminating virtuous conduct is the gateway to morality and righteousness,
substantial will and spirit are the root of talent and wisdom.)
He also sighed over the Mean to distinguish the virtue of sages,
(The virtue of the Mean,
is it not supreme?
People have rarely possessed it for long,
only sages can achieve it.)
He exalted virtue to encourage those approaching perfection.
(That disciple Yán,
came close to perfection!
Not departing from benevolence for three months,
he glimpsed the gateway of virtuous conduct.
If not for the aspiring nature of determined scholars and benevolent persons striving forward,
those who only reach it occasionally,
how could they sustain it?)
He instructed on the six蔽 to warn against the faults of偏材.
(The benevolent love all things,
their fault lies in indecisiveness;
the trustworthy reveal sincerity,
their fault lies in having no concealment.
These are common faults of偏材.)
He considered the ardent and the cautious to connect restrained and assertive talents.
(Some advance pursuing morality and righteousness,
some purify themselves and practice non-action.
Those above should accommodate both according to their abilities,
then both restrained and assertive can be employed.)
He detested superficial sincerity without trustworthiness,
to clarify how semblance is difficult to maintain.
(Thick appearance and deep feelings,
even sages find difficult to discern.
Listen to their words and observe their actions,
then false pretenses cannot escape.)
He also said: examine what they dwell in,
observe how they proceed,
to know their conduct in dwelling and resting.
(Words must accord from start to finish,
actions must be observed from beginning to end,
then inner and outer circumstances can roughly be seen.)
The examination of character and talent
should be as detailed as this.
(Without detailed examination, official talents lose their proper order,
and the work of various administrations becomes neglected.)
Therefore, I dare to follow the sage's teachings,
and record and categorize people and talents,
hoping to patch up omissions and forgetfulness.
May the broadly knowledgeable noble person judge and examine its meaning.
Chapter One: The Nine Manifestations
(People's dispositions and temperaments,
their aspirations and energies, differ.
The spirit is revealed in the countenance,
and there are nine forms of physical verification.)
Chapter One: The Nine Manifestations
The foundation of human character
stems from innate disposition.
(Inherent nature is endowed naturally,
while emotional changes arise from acquired influences.
Thus when observing people and examining things,
one should seek their inherent qualities.)
The principles of disposition and nature
are subtle and profound;
if not for the discernment of sages,
who could thoroughly investigate them?
(Knowledge has no form,
so ordinary people cannot perceive it—
only sages can witness and illuminate it.)
All living beings
contain the primordial unity as their substance,
(without this substance, they could not endure cold and heat
or pass through the four seasons.)
They receive yīn and yáng to establish their nature,
(since nature draws from yīn and yáng,
distinctions between firmness and softness arise.)
They embody the five phases to manifest form.
(The strength of bones and pliancy of sinews
all derive essence from metal and wood.)
If there is form and substance,
one can still approach and seek them.
(As vitality and complexion manifest outwardly,
physiognomists can grasp their true essence.)
In human nature,
the state of balanced harmony is the most precious.
(Just as a plain background can receive colors,
and a sweet taste can blend with other flavors.
Balanced harmony is
the foundation of all conduct,
and the fertile soil of human emotions.)
A nature characterized by balanced harmony
must be placid and flavorless,
(for only through blandness
can the five flavors achieve harmony.
If it were bitter,
it could not be sweet;
if it were sour,
it could not be salty.)
Thus it can harmonize the five talents,
and adapt flexibly to changing circumstances.
(Being placid and unbiased,
it can command all talents,
employ them appropriately,
and navigate changes without obstruction.)
Therefore, when observing a person's nature,
one must first examine their placidity,
and then seek their intelligence.
(Like a fine steed,
though it may surpass and excel beyond the herd,
if its temperament is not harmonious,
it will inevitably meet with disasters such as breaking its bit, smashing its head, or bursting its chest.)
Intelligence is
the essence of yīn and yáng.
(The eyes correspond to Lí and ears to Kǎn,
from which sight and hearing originate.)
When yīn and yáng are clear and harmonious,
then inner wisdom and outer clarity are achieved.
The sage, pure and brilliant,
can embody both beauties.
Knowing the subtle and the evident,
(with eyes and ears both observant,
penetrating the obscure and reaching the minute,
assigning positions according to talent and providing direction,
leaving nothing overlooked.)
Unless one is a sage,
none can achieve both.
(Though one may grasp with the eyes,
one might miss with the ears.)
Thus, the clear-sighted individual
understands the dynamics of action,
but is blind to profound contemplation;
(adept at advancing,
but unaware of stillness.
Using this for advancement,
they rush and cause haste-induced errors;
using it for deep thought,
they resist and fail to internalize.)
The profoundly contemplative person
recognizes the source of stillness,
but struggles with swiftness.
(Naturally inclined to silence,
their wisdom lacks responsiveness.
Employed in tranquility,
they construct the way of subtle mystery;
employed in aiding the world,
they are stiff and ineffective.)
Just as fire and the sun shine outward,
but cannot illuminate inward;
metal and water reflect inwardly,
but cannot glow outwardly.
(Each person has their abilities,
each thing its nature.
Thus, the sage entrusts action to the clear-sighted,
and assigns preservation to the profoundly contemplative,
so that movement and rest are properly regulated,
and engagement or withdrawal are appropriately timed.)
The distinction between these two
lies in the difference between yīn and yáng.
(Yáng moves, yīn is still,
this is the fixed nature of heaven and earth,
how much more so for people and things?)
If we measure their innate qualities
and examine them through the five elements,
the manifestations of these five elements
are each distinctly revealed in their corresponding bodily aspects.
(Tendons of courage show in a blue complexion,
blood of courage shows in a red complexion,
internal movements manifest externally,
how could they be concealed?)
In the body,
wood corresponds to bones, metal to tendons, fire to breath, earth to flesh, and water to blood,
which are the images of the five elements.
(These five natures
are the means through which form is constituted.
The five elements serve as the mother,
so breath and complexion follow from them and are thus provided.)
The substance of the five elements
each contributes to specific endowments.
The five natures differ,
each endowed with distinct characteristics,
and when one nature is endowed in excess, bias in character arises.
Therefore, bones that are firm yet supple
are called magnanimous and resolute;
magnanimity and resoluteness
are the substance of benevolence.
Wood spreads shade,
serving as the substance of benevolence.
If the substance lacks magnanimity and resoluteness,
it cannot achieve benevolence.
Breath that is clear and bright
is called cultured and orderly;
cultured orderliness
is the foundation of propriety.
Fire illuminates and examines,
serving as the foundation of propriety.
If the foundation lacks cultured orderliness,
it cannot achieve propriety.
A body that is upright and solid
is called steadfast and firm;
steadfastness and firmness
are the basis of trustworthiness.
Earth necessarily brings forth life,
serving as the basis of trustworthiness.
If the basis is not steadfast and firm,
it cannot achieve trustworthiness.
Tendons that are strong and refined
are called courageous and bold;
courage and boldness
are the decisiveness of righteousness.
Metal can cut and sever,
serving as the decisiveness of righteousness.
If decisiveness lacks courage and boldness,
it cannot achieve righteousness.
A complexion that is even and flowing
is called penetrating and subtle;
penetrating subtlety
is the origin of wisdom.
Water flows freely and reaches far,
serving as the origin of wisdom.
If the origin does not penetrate subtly,
it cannot achieve wisdom.
These five qualities are constant in nature,
hence they are called the five constant virtues.
The five elements
are the constant energies of heaven and earth;
the five virtues
are the constant conduct of humans and creatures.
The distinctions of the five constants
are arranged as the five virtues:
Thus, being gentle yet straightforward and tame yet resolute
is the virtue of wood;
if gentle but not straightforward, it becomes timid,
if tame but not resolute, it becomes broken.
Being firm yet solid and broad yet resolute
is the virtue of metal;
if firm but not solid, it becomes rash,
if broad but not resolute, it becomes deficient.
Being sincere yet respectful and orderly yet reverent
is the virtue of water;
if sincere but not respectful, it becomes perverse,
if orderly but not reverent, it becomes chaotic.
Being tolerant yet stern and soft yet established
is the virtue of earth;
if tolerant but not stern, it becomes negligent,
if soft but not established, it becomes scattered.
Being simple yet fluent and clear yet piercing
is the virtue of fire.
If simple but not fluent, it becomes stagnant,
if clear but not piercing, it becomes obscured.
Although the manifestations of form vary infinitely,
they still rely on these five substances.
Human emotions transform in myriad ways,
impossible to exhaust fully.
Tracing back to the source,
it often lies in these five.
Hence, the signs of firmness and softness, clarity and fluency, steadfastness and solidity
are evident in one's appearance and form,
apparent in one's voice and countenance,
and emanate through one's emotional essence,
each according to its image.
This is the natural principle,
where the spirit moves and the form manifests.
Sincerity arises from within,
and the radiance of virtue shines outwardly.
Thus, if the nature of the heart is bright and upright,
its demeanor is strong and firm;
if the nature of the heart is decisive and resolute,
its demeanor is advancing and fierce;
if the nature of the heart is calm and orderly,
its demeanor is tranquil and leisurely.
Now, the movements of demeanor form expressions,
each with its own attitude:
the movement of a straightforward demeanor
is vigorous and resolute;
the movement of a refined demeanor
is diligent and poised;
the movement of a virtuous demeanor
is dignified and lofty.
The movements of one's countenance
originate from the heart's energy,
which resides within,
while the countenance manifests externally.
The signs of the heart's energy
are reflected in the variations of the voice.
If the heart is not focused,
the harmony of the voice will change.
When energy combines to form sound,
the sound corresponds to the musical pitches:
clear and bright tones are lǜ,
harmonious and even tones are lǚ.
There are peaceful and harmonious voices,
clear and fluent voices,
and winding and expansive voices.
As the heart's energy differs,
so too do the sounds produced vary.
When the voice flows smoothly through energy,
it reflects the substance in one's appearance and expression:
without energy, no sound can form,
and once sound is formed, the appearance responds.
Thus, genuine benevolence
must have a gentle and kind expression;
genuine courage
must have a resolute and vigorous expression;
genuine wisdom
must have a clear and perceptive expression.
Since voices differ like pipes,
expressions also vary in form.
The expression seen in the countenance
is what is called the manifestation of spirit.
The speed and ease of one's expression
serve as evidence of the spirit.
When the spirit is revealed in the countenance,
then emotions emanate from the eyes.
The eyes are the windows to the heart,
so they respond and express according to the heart.
Therefore, in benevolence,
the essence of the eyes
is sincere and upright;
if the heart is not biased,
the gaze will not be evasive.
In courage,
the essence of the gallbladder
is bright and strong.
If the will is not timid,
the gaze will not appear weary or dejected.
However, these are all partial talents,
relying on a predominant physical nature.
They cannot be authoritative without severity,
nor stern without anger.
Thus, if the predominant nature is not refined,
one's endeavors will not succeed.
Being able to be brave but not cautious,
every action will be followed by regret and hardship.
Hence, being straightforward without flexibility makes one rigid;
rigid and forceful in exposing faults
loses true integrity.
Being strong without refinement makes one rely on brute force;
carrying a tripod until the tendons snap
loses proper strength.
Being stubborn without uprightness leads to foolishness;
self-absorbed and self-righteous,
one falls into obstinate stupidity.
Having energy without clarity leads to excess;
speech unclear and不顺,
results in chaotic and unproductive outbursts.
Being fluent without balance leads to recklessness;
loving wisdom without limits,
one becomes wildly lost.
Therefore, the nature of the Mean
differs from these types.
Brave yet able to be cautious,
benevolent yet able to decide,
embodying both qualities,
thus it is the master of all talents.
With the five constant virtues fully present,
they are enveloped in a bland flavor.
Having embodied the measures of saltiness and sourness,
it uses tastelessness as its guide.
The five substances充实 within,
the five essences manifest outwardly.
The five substances serene and凝结,
their pure radiance shines brilliantly externally.
Thus, the eyes gleam with the light of five hues.
With a clear heart and bright eyes,
they sparkle and shine on their own.
Therefore, it is said, "All living things have form,
and form has spirit and essence."
Regardless of wisdom or folly,
all receive their innate nature from the endowments of yīn and yáng,
but wisdom can be refined or coarse,
and forms can be shallow or deep.
By seeking their essential expressions,
and observing their demeanor and appearance,
down to the lowliest servants and herdsmen,
one can understand them through reflection.
Those who can comprehend the spirit and essence
will exhaust principles and fully realize nature.
The sages had the means to observe the movements of the world and liken them to forms and appearances,
thus they could exhaust principles and fully realize nature, reaching the decree of Heaven.
The nature's ultimate expression
manifests through nine essential qualities.
As yīn and yáng generate each other,
their numerical limit is nine.
Thus the variations in disposition and nature
correspond to these qualities.
Now, the quality of balance or imbalance lies in spirit;
spirit
is the master of qualities.
Therefore when spirit is balanced, qualities are balanced;
when spirit is imbalanced, qualities are imbalanced.
The substance of brightness or dimness lies in essence;
essence
is the foundation of substance.
Thus when essence is clear, substance is bright;
when essence is turbid, substance is dim.
The disposition toward courage or timidity lies in sinews;
sinews
determine the application of disposition.
Therefore when sinews are firm, disposition is courageous;
when sinews are weak, disposition is timid.
The establishment of strength or weakness lies in bones;
bones
are the foundation of establishment.
Thus when bones are hard, establishment is strong;
when bones are soft, establishment is weak.
The decision between agitation and calm lies in breath;
breath
is the ground for decision.
When breath is vigorous, decision tends toward agitation;
when breath is harmonious, decision tends toward calm.
The feelings of sorrow or joy lie in complexion;
complexion
is the indicator of feelings.
Thus haggard complexion comes from sorrowful feelings;
cheerful complexion comes from joyful feelings.
The form of decline or uprightness lies in demeanor;
demeanor
is the manifestation of form.
Thus declining demeanor comes from perilous form;
upright demeanor comes from solemn form.
The movement of attitude lies in appearance;
appearance
is the sign of movement.
Therefore devious movement shows in affected appearance;
proper movement shows in measured appearance.
The state of slowness or urgency lies in speech.
Speech
is the expression of heart.
Thus when heart is tolerant, speech is slow;
when heart is narrow, speech is urgent.
When a person
possesses plain and tranquil qualities,
wise within and bright without,
with firm sinews and solid bones,
clear voice and cheerful complexion,
elevated demeanor and upright appearance,
then all nine qualities are present,
making perfect virtue.
If not the great person of ultimate virtue,
who could attain this?
When the nine qualities are deficient,
deficiency means discord.
Then it becomes biased and mixed talent.
Some may have clear voice and cheerful complexion,
yet qualities are not plain;
some may have firm sinews and solid bones,
yet demeanor is not elevated and upright.
The three measures differ,
their virtues have different names.
Biased talent bears the name of single excellence,
combined talent occupies the category of virtue and demeanor,
combined virtue embodies the measure of the golden mean.
Thus biased talent of single excellence
is named for its specific talent;
like various crafts and skills,
each has its own name.
People of combined talent
are categorized by virtue;
benevolence, righteousness, propriety, and wisdom -
they attain one category.
People of combined virtue
receive even more honorable titles.
The Way cannot be explained through one form,
virtue cannot be treated from one perspective.
Nourishing all things yet not acting from benevolence,
equalizing all forms yet not acting from virtue.
Serenely plain and tranquil,
boundless with all things,
who can know their name?
Therefore when combined virtue reaches its peak,
it is called the golden mean;
abiding in centrality and following constancy,
thus it is called the golden mean.
The golden mean
is the designation for sages.
Great benevolence cannot be approached,
great righteousness cannot be repaid,
having no virtue that can be named,
they entrust their name to sagehood.
Having all essentials though in miniature
is called virtuous conduct;
virtuous conduct
is the designation of great refinement.
Practicing benevolence to be intimate with things,
establishing righteousness to benefit benevolence,
losing the Way yet achieving virtue -
this is still secondary.
Single excellence is called biased talent;
biased talent
is the quality of minor refinement;
having only benevolence without righteousness,
or only righteousness without benevolence,
unable to combine and benefit all,
each clinging to one practice,
thus their names fall short of great refinement.
Single quality manifestation is called semblance;
semblance
is the category of corrupted virtue;
pure criticism appears straightforward but isn't true straightforwardness,
pure indulgence appears open-minded but isn't true open-mindedness.
Both excellence and deficiency is called mixed;
mixed
refers to inconstant people.
Good and evil intermixed,
the mind lacks fixed principles.
Inconstant character
cannot be properly assessed.
Inconstant and semblance types
are both inferior followers of customs.
Those whose hearts are profoundly difficult
may not accept even education and transformation.
The qualities of inferior followers
cannot be fully discussed,
thus they are omitted and not generalized.
When followers multiply into groups,
how can they be counted!
On the Distinctions of Character, Part Two
Endowed with the qi of yin and yang,
Nature has strength and gentleness.
Constrained or unyielding, refined or plain,
Forms of character differ distinctly.
"Varieties of Temperament" Part Two
The virtue of the Mean,
its essence is nameless.
Vast and unbound to any single appearance,
people cannot find words to praise it.
Thus, it is salty but not briny—
if called salty,
there is no brininess to be found;
just as public success accommodates all flavors, it aligns with saltiness.
Bland but not insipid—
if called bland,
its taste is not insipid.
Simple but not coarse—
if called simple,
its principle is not coarsely plain.
Cultured but not ornate—
if called cultured,
its elegance is not painted with embellishment.
It can inspire awe and win hearts,
can articulate clearly or remain reticent,
dwelling in the harmony of saltiness and blandness,
residing at the junction of simplicity and refinement.
Therefore, from afar, it appears dignified;
up close, it is refined,
its words fill the world without waste.
It changes without fixed rules,
guided by the principle of attainment.
Adapting to transformations and responding to changes,
it aims to connect with all things.
Thus, the assertive go beyond it,
vigorously striving on the path of advancement,
while the restrained fall short,
remaining stagnant in inaction beyond both restraint and assertiveness.
When restraint and assertiveness deviate from the mean,
some strengths become evident,
while principles are lost.
Nurturing the body excessively
invites tigers to devour from without;
lofty gates and thin curtains
allow illness to assail from within.
Thus, stern integrity and resolute fortitude
excel in rectifying wrongs,
but fail in being overly critical;
harsh criticism arises from rigid severity.
Gentle compliance and forgiving patience
often manifest in tolerance,
but fail in indecisiveness;
excessive doubt stems from timid leniency.
Bold fierceness and heroic vigor
shine in courageous fervor,
but fail in harboring many suspicions;
contempt for laws springs from reckless brutality.
Refined vigilance and cautious fear
excel in reverence and prudence,
but fail in excessive hesitation;
perplexing difficulties arise from fearful caution.
Strong principles and unyielding firmness
serve as pillars of support,
but fail in stubborn obstinacy;
self-absorption stems from rigid strength.
Debating and unraveling reasoning
can resolve complexities,
but fail in drifting aimlessly;
arrogant waywardness arises from clever arguments.
Universal knowledge and comprehensive mastery
broaden through encompassing generosity,
but fail in muddled confusion;
turbidity arises from all-encompassing breadth.
Pure integrity and incorruptible honesty
uphold thrift and steadfastness,
but fail in narrow confinement;
restriction stems from uncompromising廉洁.
Active dynamism and open-hearted magnanimity
thrive in climbing heights,
but fail in careless overstepping;
negligent excess arises from unconstrained openness.
Deep tranquility and secretive discretion
excel in profound subtlety,
but fail in sluggish delay;
slowness arises from serene calmness.
Simple revelation and direct exhaustiveness
embody inner sincerity,
but fail in lacking subtlety;
exposure stems from straightforward completeness.
Abundant wisdom and concealed emotions
wield power in strategic cunning,
but fail in wavering indecision.
Hidden contradictions arise from emotional restraint.
When the days of advancing virtue do not cease,
measuring by the中庸之道 warns against the extremes of restraint and assertiveness in one's talents.
The assertive thus strive with vigor,
while the restrained thus hold to their limits.
Yet pointing out others' shortcomings to amplify their faults
makes the restrained more confined,
and the assertive more extreme.
Some may carry stones to sink themselves,
others cling to trees and wither to death.
It is like the people of Jìn and Chǔ wearing swords,
each deeming the other's way contrary.
Viewed from Jìn,
they laugh at Chǔ for wearing it on the left;
viewed from Chǔ,
they laugh at Jìn for wearing it on the right.
Though left and right differ,
each has its utility,
yet those who fail to understand the principle
recklessly slander one another.
The opposition between restraint and assertiveness
is no different from this.
Therefore, those who are strong and resolute,
are fierce, rigid, and unyielding,
and do not guard against the aggressiveness of their strength,
but see compliance as weakness,
intensify their resistance.
Taking gentleness and compliance as feeble submission,
they reinforce their aggressive tendencies.
Thus, they can establish laws,
but find it hard to grasp subtleties.
Being fierce, strong, rigid, and harsh,
how can they penetrate delicate matters?
Gentle and compliant individuals,
are lax-minded and lenient in judgment,
and do not guard against their lack of control in affairs,
but see resistance as harmful,
and indulge in their ease.
Viewing fierce resistance as injurious,
they nurture their forgiving and tolerant hearts.
Thus, they can follow routines,
but find it hard to handle doubtful situations.
With a lax mind and indecisiveness,
how can they weigh uncertain matters?
Bold and fierce individuals,
with spirited courage and decisive actions,
do not guard against the risks of their bravery,
but see compliance as timidity,
and exhaust their momentum.
Taking compliance and tolerance as cowardice,
they deplete their potential to avoid pitfalls.
Thus, they can face difficulties,
but find it hard to live in restraint.
Being impetuous, fierce, and prone to missteps,
how can they abide by constraints?
Cautious and fearful individuals,
wary of troubles and full of inhibitions,
do not guard against their timidity in upholding righteousness,
but see courage as recklessness,
and increase their doubts.
Viewing brave steadfastness as frivolous disrespect,
they amplify their suspicious and fearful hearts.
Thus, they can preserve safety,
but find it hard to establish moral integrity.
Wary of troubles and full of inhibitions,
how can they uphold principles and righteousness?
Upright and principled individuals,
firm in will and resolute,
do not guard against the obstinacy of their sentiments,
but see debate as deceit,
and reinforce their rigidity.
Taking eloquent debate as superficial falsity,
they strengthen their single-minded focus.
Thus, they can uphold justice,
but find it hard to win over the masses.
Stubborn and unyielding,
how can they attract followers?
Eloquent and knowledgeable individuals,
abundant in reasoning and articulate,
do not guard against the excesses of their words,
but see principles as constraints,
and indulge in their flow.
Viewing principled correctness as hindrance,
they follow their wandering inclinations.
Thus, they can discuss broadly,
but find it hard to establish firm agreements.
With broad but overflowing discourse,
how can they set substantial limits?
Broad-minded and inclusive individuals,
with compassionate and extensive affections,
do not guard against the chaos of their associations,
but see integrity as narrow-mindedness,
and expand their muddledness.
Taking strict integrity as obstinate harshness,
they broaden their confused and mixed intentions.
Thus, they can comfort the masses,
but find it hard to refine customs.
With all-encompassing yet chaotic associations,
how can they improve social morals?
Incorruptible and principled individuals,
criticizing
(fǔ, pronounced as in "fǔ lián"),
purity and stirring up turbidity,
do not guard against the narrowness of their path,
but see inclusivity as filth,
and deepen their rigidity.
Viewing broad inclusivity as dirty mixture,
they intensify their confined and limited minds.
Thus, they can uphold integrity,
but find it hard to adapt flexibly.
With a narrow path and restricted access,
how can they traverse open roads?
Active and dynamic individuals,
aspiring to surpass and excel,
do not guard against the excessiveness of their ambitions,
but see stillness as stagnation,
and sharpen their edge.
Taking calmness as suppression,
they enhance their determined and sharp spirits.
Thus, they can advance and strive,
but find it hard to maintain restraint.
With ambitions set on surpassing,
how can they uphold humility and caution?
Calm and quiet individuals,
contemplating deeply and repeatedly,
do not guard against the slowness of their stillness,
but see action as negligence,
and praise their timidity.
Viewing impulsiveness as recklessness,
they glorify their timid hearts.
Thus, they can plan deeply,
but find it hard to act swiftly.
With thoughts circling and recurring,
how can they keep up with rapid opportunities?
Simple and straightforward individuals,
sincerely doubtful and genuinely solid,
do not guard against the rustic bluntness of their honesty,
but see cunning as absurdity,
and reveal their sincerity.
Taking strategic cunning as frivolous deception,
they expose their honest and faithful hearts.
Thus, they can build trust,
but find it hard to adapt to changes.
With genuine solidity and rustic directness,
how can they measure the weight of matters?
Reserved and cunning individuals,
adapting to please others,
do not guard against the deviation of their methods from righteousness,
but see sincerity as foolishness,
and value their emptiness.
Taking wholehearted sincerity as naive straightforwardness,
they prize their superficial and hollow minds.
Thus, they can praise goodness,
but find it hard to correct wrongs.
With reserved cunning straying from righteousness,
how can they rectify deviations and evils?
Learning is the means to cultivate talent;
it strengthens the resolute and calms their aggressiveness,
and tempers the gentle to overcome their timidity.
Forgiveness is the means to extend empathy;
by projecting one's own feelings,
one understands the nature of others.
Yet the inherent nature of a biased talent cannot be altered.
Firmly clinging to their innate disposition,
they hear righteousness but do not change.
Even if taught through learning,
once talent is formed, it is accompanied by flaws.
When a rigid and unyielding nature is established,
a tendency to criticize and expose becomes even more entrenched.
Even if instructed in forgiveness,
the extension of empathy follows their own inclinations.
What they disapprove of in their minds,
they refuse to affirm in others.
The trustworthy suspect trustworthiness in others,
projecting their own honesty onto everyone,
thus allowing the deceitful to feign integrity.
The deceitful suspect deceit in others,
projecting their own cunning onto everyone,
so the honest may be wrongly doubted.
Therefore, if learning does not lead to the Way,
and forgiveness does not encompass all things,
biased individuals,
each convinced of their own abilities,
how can they enter the Way,
or be comprehensive in their understanding?
This is the increasing failure of biased talents.
When talent is not versatile,
teaching only exacerbates the shortcomings.
Hence, those who govern should employ a person's benevolence while curbing their greed,
and use their wisdom while eliminating their deceit.
Only then can all talents be fully utilized,
and the Way be comprehensive in all things.
On the Flow of Professions, the Third
Three talents are the source,
habitual practice forms the flow.
As the flow gradually loses the source,
their professions each differ.
〈Flowing Careers〉 Third
There are twelve types of professions among human talents.
As their innate natures differ,
and acquired habits vary,
branches and streams diverge,
each with its own aspirations and occupations.
There are the Qīngjiéjiā,
whose conduct serves as models for all.
There are the Fǎjiā,
who establish constitutions and institute systems.
There are the Shùjiā,
whose wisdom and strategies know no bounds.
There are the Guótǐ,
who possess all three talents in pure form.
There are the Qìnéng,
who have the three talents but to a lesser degree.
There are the Zāngpǐ,
who distinguish right from wrong.
There are the Jìliǎng,
who focus on skill and ingenuity.
There are the Zhìyì,
who can resolve the doubts of the masses.
There are the Wénzhāng,
who compose writings and narrate events.
There are the Rúxué,
who deeply understand the Way and arts.
There are the Kǒubiàn,
who respond with wit and agility.
There are the Xióngjié.
whose courage and strategy surpass others.
As for those with lofty virtue and conduct,
whose demeanor is worthy of emulation,
they are called the Pure and Upright school,
exemplified by Yánlíng and Yàn Yīng.
Establishing laws and institutions,
strengthening the state and enriching the people,
they are called the Legalist school,
exemplified by Guǎn Zhòng and Shāng Yāng.
Thinking that comprehends the Way and its transformations,
with ingenious strategies and plans,
they are called the Strategist school,
exemplified by Fàn Lǐ and Zhāng Liáng.
Combining all three talents,
with all three talents fully developed,
virtue, law,
and strategy all complete and pure.
Their virtue is sufficient to inspire customs,
their laws to rectify the world,
their strategies to plan victory in the court,
they are called the Pillars of the State,
exemplified by Yī Yǐn and Lǚ Wàng.
Combining all three talents,
but with all three talents only slightly developed,
not fully complete.
Their virtue is sufficient to lead a state,
their laws to rectify towns and cities,
their strategies to handle affairs appropriately,
they are called the Capable and Useful,
exemplified by Zǐchǎn and Xīmén Bào.
Combining variations of the three talents,
each with its own stream.
The three talents are the source,
then those who learn them form the streams.
The stream of the Pure and Upright,
cannot be broadly tolerant,
governing with purity,
how can they be lenient?
Fond of criticizing and reproaching,
distinguishing right from wrong,
if they themselves are not tolerant,
then judgments of right and wrong arise.
They are called the Critical,
exemplified by the followers of Zǐxià.
The stream of the Legalists,
cannot create far-reaching plans,
their legal system is limited to the near,
their thoughts do not reach far.
But they can undertake the duties of an office,
applying their minds with skill,
focused on achieving success,
hence their ingenuity arises.
They are called the Tacticians,
exemplified by Zhāng Chǎng and Zhào Guǎnghàn.
The stream of the Strategists,
cannot establish institutions and set examples,
seeking achievement through strategy,
thus they do not set examples.
But they can adapt to change using expediency,
with ample tactical wisdom,
but insufficient impartiality,
those skilled in expediency,
must be lacking in righteousness.
They are called the Wise and Astute,
exemplified by Chén Píng and Hán Ānguó.
All these eight professions,
are based on the three talents.
Without virtue, there is no way to rectify laws,
without laws, there is no way to promote strategy.
Thus the establishment of these eight professions,
always relies on the three talents as foundation.
So although they branch into different streams,
all are talents for managing affairs.
Ears and eyes have different functions,
but their use achieves the same purpose;
various talents may differ,
but accomplishing tasks unites them.
Those capable of writing and composing works,
are called the Literary,
exemplified by Sīmǎ Qiān and Bān Gù.
Those capable of transmitting the works of sages,
but not of handling affairs and administering government,
are called the Confucian Scholars,
exemplified by Máo Gōng and Guǎn Gōng.
Debate that does not enter the Way,
but with responsive and resourceful replies,
are called the Eloquent,
exemplified by Yuè Yì and Cáo Qiūshēng.
With courage and strength surpassing all,
and talent and strategy exceeding others,
are called the Valiant and Heroic,
exemplified by Bái Qǐ and Hán Xìn.
All these twelve types of talent,
constitute the responsibilities of ministers,
each upholding their own talent,
unable to be comprehensive,
preserving a single office,
thus they are the responsibilities of ministers.
The virtue of the ruler is not included here.
The virtue of a ruler lies in being intelligent and unassuming,
overseeing all talents comprehensively,
without taking on tasks personally.
The eyes do not seek to see everything,
the ears do not interfere with listening,
each organ performs its own function,
thus all talents are fully utilized.
Once all talents are fully utilized,
the ruler can govern with ease and inaction.
Therefore, when the way of the ruler is established,
the twelve types of talents each find their appropriate roles.
If the ruler practices inaction,
the subordinates will fulfill their duties accordingly.
The virtue of purity and integrity
suits the role of the Shīshì;
responsible for morality,
educating the noble youth.
The talent of the Legalist school
fits the role of the Sīkòu;
in charge of penal laws,
prohibiting wickedness and violence.
The talent of the Strategist school
suits the role of the Sāngū;
responsible for temple strategies,
assisting in public deliberation and correction.
When the three talents are pure and complete,
they suit the role of the Sāngōng;
positioned at the three locust trees,
sitting to discuss the Way.
When the three talents are subtle,
they suit the role of the Zhǒngzǎi;
the minister of the Ministry of Heaven,
overseeing all officials.
The talent of judgment
assists the Shīshì;
distinguishing right from wrong,
to aid the Shīshì.
The talent of wisdom and insight
assists the Zhǒngzǎi;
adapting to circumstances appropriately,
to aid the Ministry of Heaven.
The talent of skill and craft
suits the role of the Sīkōng;
focusing on applying ingenuity,
hence in charge of the Ministry of Winter.
The talent of Confucian learning
suits the role of pacifying the people;
responsible for virtue and sustenance,
ensuring their safety and well-being.
The talent of literary composition
suits the role of the state historian;
documenting laws and records,
passing them down to future generations.
The talent of eloquence
suits the role of the envoy;
responsible for responses,
greeting and sending off on the roads.
The talent of bravery and heroism
suits the role of the general;
in command of armies,
suppressing disobedience.
This is called the way of the ruler being achieved and the way of the ministers being orderly,
officials not changing their methods,
thus achieving great peace.
The reason great peace is achieved
lies in the officials not altering their ways.
If the feet were to grasp objects,
and the hands sought to walk,
how could the four limbs find peace?
How could the way of governance be balanced?
If the way is not unassuming,
but instead favors one talent exclusively,
it is like a master craftsman skilled with the compass,
using only the compass.
Then one talent holds power,
and all other talents lose their roles.
If only the compass is used,
the square cannot establish its form,
the ink line cannot draw straight,
and even if the compass and square are used daily,
nothing can be accomplished.
On Abilities and Principles, Fourth
Abilities follow different paths,
principles also diverge in their directions.
Thus, when discussing the multitude of talents,
the ultimate principles are established.
"On the Nature of Talent and Principle" Fourth
In establishing affairs and setting forth principles,
none can be determined without reason.
When words are settled beforehand, there is no confusion;
when matters are decided in advance, there is no stumbling.
Yet when it comes to debate and contention,
few are able to settle them.
What is the reason for this?
It is because principles vary in kind and human talents differ.
Affairs are innumerable,
human dispositions are contradictory and complex—
who can settle them?
Now, the multiplicity of principles makes them hard to comprehend;
the diversity of human talents leads to erratic dispositions.
With erratic dispositions and principles hard to comprehend,
reason is lost and affairs go awry.
With dispositions erratic and principles numerous,
how can one attain understanding?
Now, principles fall into four categories:
the Way, righteousness, affairs, and circumstances—
each has its category.
Clarity of understanding has four schools;
those who comprehend the four categories clearly
each belong to their respective school.
Dispositions have nine biases;
when dispositions interfere with clarity,
there are nine types of gains and losses.
There are seven forms of superficial resemblance;
appearing right yet being wrong—
their manifestations are seven.
Persuasion has three faults;
when rhetoric overpowers reason and logic stagnates,
the failures are three.
Disputes involve six conflicts;
when the strong and capable contend in spirit,
the resulting resentments form six patterns.
Mastery encompasses eight abilities;
with acute thought and clear comprehension,
those who achieve mastery possess eight capacities.
As for the transformation of the energies of heaven and earth,
their fullness and emptiness, decrease and increase,
are the principles of the Way;
to transform people with the Way,
one must adapt with the times, waxing and waning.
Laws and institutions govern affairs properly,
which are the principles of affairs;
to manage people with laws,
one must focus on constitutional order.
Ritual teachings should be appropriate,
which are the principles of righteousness;
to educate with these principles,
ensures that actions and cessations are fitting.
The pivotal mechanisms of human emotions,
are the principles of feelings.
To observe the sentiments of things,
lies in speech and language.
The four principles differ;
regarding talent,
it must be illuminated to manifest,
and illumination depends on substance to act.
Thus, when substance aligns with principle,
alignment brings illumination,
illumination suffices to reveal principle,
and principle suffices to establish a school.
Morality and practical affairs each have their schools.
Hence, those with a calm and plain substance,
a mind inclined to profound subtleties,
and a demeanor free from agitation,
possess a detailed and meticulous heart.
They can comprehend nature—
these are the school of the Way and principle;
taking the Way as principle,
thus they can comprehend nature.
Those with an alert and clear substance,
tactical acumen and quick-wittedness,
and a demeanor that is never sluggish,
then their minds are swift and strategic.
They can manage complexities and urgencies—
these are the school of affairs and principle;
taking affairs as principle,
thus they are adept at handling troubles.
Those with a harmonious and balanced substance,
capable of discussing rites and teachings,
and a demeanor that never loses appropriateness,
then the rites and teachings achieve moderation.
They debate gains and losses—
these are the school of righteousness and principle;
taking righteousness as principle,
thus they are clear about merits and faults.
Those with an astute and perceptive substance,
inferring emotions and tracing intentions,
and a demeanor that avoids rash actions,
then they grasp the essence of things.
They can adapt to changes—
these are the school of emotion and principle.
Taking emotion as principle,
thus they can exhaust the transformations of things.
Since the understanding of these four schools differs,
there arise nine biased dispositions.
When dispositions override understanding,
each has its gains and losses.
Understanding emerges from authenticity,
while dispositions are stirred by nature.
When dispositions overpower understanding, obscurity follows—
thus even gains are inevitably lost.
Those of bold and broad nature
cannot handle subtleties.
Their thinking is coarse and neglectful,
lacking depth and refinement.
Thus in discussing grand principles,
they appear expansive and lofty;
their resolute nature breeds lofty ambitions.
Yet when tracing fine details,
they become erratic and overlook intricacies.
Lofty ambitions lead to oversights.
Those of stern and severe nature
cannot yield or compromise.
Their thinking is fiercely driven,
unyielding in purpose.
In discussing laws and integrity,
they are rigorous and impartial;
their severity fosters steadfast judgment.
But in addressing adaptability,
they become obstinate and inflexible.
Steadfast judgment leads to rigidity.
Those of firm and resolute nature
prefer to confront facts directly.
Their thinking is straightforward and precise,
leaving no room for ambiguity.
In analyzing mechanisms and principles,
they are sharp and exhaustive;
their precision ensures thorough expression.
Yet when approaching profound truths,
they become blunt and one-sided.
Directness diminishes depth of meaning.
Those of eloquent and quick-witted nature
use copious words with sharp intent.
Their thinking is swift and urgent,
unyielding to setbacks.
In analyzing human affairs,
they exhibit keen insight and exhaustive reasoning;
their sharpness pursues logical extremes.
But when confronting grand principles,
they become startlingly incomplete.
Attention to minutiae neglects the greater whole.
Those of floating and drifting nature
cannot engage in deep contemplation.
Their thinking is vague and boundless,
lacking profound focus.
In arranging scattered matters,
they appear open-minded yet arrogantly broad;
their superficiality breeds conceited aims.
Yet in establishing crucial tasks,
they flicker uncertainly like flames.
Conceited aims lead to shallow reasoning.
Those of shallow comprehension
cannot probe deeply or challenge rigorously.
Their thinking is superficial and fleeting,
lacking depth and maturity.
When hearing persuasive arguments,
they mimic sharpness with delight;
their shallowness makes them easily pleased.
But when examining refined principles,
they waver without foundation.
Easy pleasure leaves them rootless.
Those of tolerant and forgiving nature
cannot act swiftly or decisively.
Their thinking is slow and gradual,
lacking urgency.
In discussing benevolence and righteousness,
they are comprehensive and elegantly profound;
their forgiving nature fosters refined reasoning.
Yet in pursuing timely matters,
they lag behind, unable to keep pace.
Slowness and refinement cause delay.
Those of gentle and soft nature
lack forceful strength.
Their thinking is warm and smooth,
without fierce determination.
In savoring truths and principles,
they follow smoothly and harmoniously;
their gentleness aligns with logical flow.
But when facing doubts and difficulties,
they become timid and indecisive.
Alignment leads to wavering.
Those of curious and unconventional nature
leap beyond norms seeking novelty.
Their thinking is peculiar and unique,
diverging from common views.
In crafting strategic deception,
they are dashing and magnificently bold;
their oddity崇尚华丽.
Yet in examining pure principles,
they distort conventions and become absurdly circuitous.
Eccentricity breeds诡谲.
These are the so-called nine biased dispositions,
each following what the mind deems reasonable.
When the mind’s inclinations define rationality,
right and wrong obscure each other—
an endless cycle without cessation.
If one's nature is not refined and fluent,
then there emerge seven semblances:
Some engage in rambling discourses and stale statements,
appearing as if they are in vogue;
superficial and diffuse yet elegant,
seemingly practicable.
Some have scant reasoning but numerous aspects,
appearing as if they encompass broad ideas;
with elaborate rhetoric and extensive analogies,
seemingly vast and comprehensive.
Some twist arguments to fit the meaning,
appearing as if they endorse understanding;
outwardly pretending to agree,
while inwardly truly ignorant.
Some stay behind and hold onto strengths,
following what the crowd finds comforting,
appearing capable of listening and judging;
actually lacking knowledge themselves,
as if saying nothing.
Observing the crowd's discussions,
praising what they find acceptable.
Some avoid difficult questions without responding,
appearing as if they have more to say,
but are actually ignorant;
truly unable to know,
pretending to forget and not responding,
seeming to have knowledge but not answering.
Some admire fluency and offer superficial explanations,
appearing pleased but not truly comprehending;
hearing words and immediately speaking,
seeming to understand,
yet their minds are muddled and unable to grasp the truth.
Some, due to emotional attachment to victory, lose their way,
when exhausted, they claim profundity;
their arguments have run out,
yet they consider them subtle and unfinished.
When their reasoning falters, they grasp at straws;
the logic has already collapsed,
yet they forcibly drag in evidence.
Truly seeking dual interpretations,
appearing as if their reasoning cannot be refuted.
Their rhetoric exhausted and logic defeated,
their minds delight in dual explanations,
and yet their speech does not cease,
listeners think they have not been defeated.
All these seven semblances,
are what confuse the masses.
Without a clear mirror, how can one discern them?
In debate, there is victory by reason,
where the reasoning is so impeccable it cannot be shaken.
There is victory by rhetoric.
where the eloquence is so skillful it cannot be refuted.
Victory by reason
clarifies black and white to broaden the argument,
explaining subtleties to make them comprehensible;
it presents matters distinctly,
as if adorned with powder and ink.
Clearly differentiated,
the discourse remains uncluttered.
Victory by rhetoric,
however, undermines sound reasoning to seek novelty,
and in seeking novelty, correctness is lost.
By claiming "a white horse is not a horse,"
one may convince a thousand people in a single morning.
But when it comes to critical prohibitions,
only straightforwardness prevails afterward.
As for the nine biased talents,
some are similar,
some are opposite,
some are mixed.
Similar ones understand each other,
like water flowing into water.
Opposite ones contradict each other,
as fire is extinguished by water.
Mixed ones accommodate each other.
They need not be identical,
nor entirely different,
thus achieving broad comprehension.
Therefore, those skilled in engaging in debate
assess the strengths of others and discuss accordingly.
By aligning with their capabilities,
their words become easily understood.
If repeated efforts yield no response,
they cease to speak;
if the other's interest lies in dogs,
horses are left for another day.
If there are no perceptive listeners nearby,
it is not forced.
Generally, engaging in difficult discussions
is for the sake of the enlightened listener.
Those unskilled in engaging in debate
speak with mixed contradictions;
the other intends to discuss dogs,
yet they speak of horses.
The other seeks broad similarities,
yet they emphasize minor differences.
Speaking with mixed contradictions,
then the message does not penetrate.
Trying to fit a square into a circle,
the principle ultimately fails.
Those skilled in illustration
clarify multiple matters with a single statement.
When words adhere to reason,
then few words make matters clear.
Those unskilled in illustration
use a hundred words without clarifying one idea.
When words stray from reason,
even if overflowing with many words,
they fail to enlighten themselves,
let alone others.
Using a hundred words without clarifying one idea,
then others will not listen.
If one's own meaning is unclear,
who will listen to it?
These are the three failures in discourse.
Those skilled in debate
focus on clarifying the root of the matter.
They stop once the principle is understood.
Those unskilled in debate
abandon the root and pursue the trivial.
They chase after words and engage with them.
By abandoning the root and pursuing the trivial,
they create disputes of rhetoric.
Not seeking the fundamental principle,
they embellish with verbose language.
Those skilled in attacking the strong
diminish their vigorous sharpness.
When the opponent is forceful,
their initial energy is bound to be intense.
Thus, those skilled in attacking the strong
avoid their initial surge.
They support the core intent
and gradually attack it.
After three surges, their energy peaks,
and when it wanes, the attack becomes easier.
Those unskilled in attacking the strong
seize on their erroneous words
to挫挫 their sharp intent;
the strong have sharp intentions,
and their words may be momentarily mistaken,
but attacking errors to挫挫 sharpness
makes reasoning difficult.
By挫挫 their sharp intent,
they create conflicts of energy.
Not only do numerous arguments intertwine,
but it even leads to agitated expressions and tones.
Those skilled at tracking errors
point out where the other has stumbled.
If the other has stumbled or erred,
they point it out temporarily without pressing.
Those unskilled at tracking errors
exploit the setback to attack their nature.
They belittle the stumble and press to挫挫 it.
By exploiting the setback to attack their nature,
they create resentment.
It's not just about expressions and tones;
hatred and resentment form inwardly.
Sometimes, after long contemplation and seeking,
one finally gains understanding.
If they hastily explain to others,
and others do not quickly grasp it,
they consider them hard to enlighten.
They themselves have long pondered but do not empathize with others.
Considering others hard to enlighten,
they create indignation.
It's not just resentment;
it leads to angry disputes.
During intense debate,
their errors are hard to press.
When energy is high and words erroneous,
one should暂且 avoid them.
Thus, those skilled in debate
guide them to retreat.
Once their energy is subdued and intent withdrawn,
they naturally respond and engage.
Those unskilled in debate
provoke and incite them;
even if they wish to show consideration,
there is no way to do so.
Abandoning errors and showing consideration,
they do not listen to the words.
With no way to do so,
they create recklessness.
Reckless words and unwarranted criticism
flow freely and unrestrained from the mouth.
Whenever people's minds are preoccupied with thought,
their ears cannot listen.
Once focused thought arrives,
they do not hear even thunder.
Therefore, when thinking and speaking simultaneously,
they compete to interrupt each other,
wanting others to listen to themselves.
Stopping others' words
to make them listen to oneself.
Others, also due to their own ongoing thoughts,
do not fully grasp one's meaning,
and so one thinks they do not understand.
It is not that they do not understand;
rather, when one speaks,
the other is still thinking,
so they do not comprehend.
Human nature tends to avoid admitting lack of understanding.
Telling them they do not understand
triggers their instinct to avoid and anger.
Avoiding lack of understanding
leads to the construction of anger.
Disregarding reason and right or wrong in their凶怒 and unrestrained fury.
All these six constructions
are the sources from which changes arise.
Although there may be alterations in structure,
something can still be gained.
When creating affairs and establishing principles,
one must base them on reason.
Thus, even with minor variations in discourse,
ultimately, reason is established and achievements are made.
If one speaks without being challenged,
and each presents their own views,
then no one knows the basis.
When everyone competes to speak,
if there is no challenge to the substance,
it becomes unclear which views are usable.
From this perspective,
those who can establish principles through discussion
are rare.
Reasons are manifold,
and human feelings differ.
Hence, even with a room full of speeches,
none are willing to take the blame.
One must have the wisdom to discern order in listening,
the ability to compose poetry when ascending heights,
and to name things when seeking them,
like Yán Huí discerning the meaning from a cry,
or Cāng Shū measuring an elephant.
The thought must be able to initiate ideas,
as Zǐ Zhǎn plotted an invasion of Jìn,
leading to alliances among the feudal lords.
Insight must perceive opportunities,
as Yú Pián observed eye movements
and knew the Qín army would retreat.
Eloquence must convey intent clearly,
as Yī Jí replied to the King of Wú,
saying that one bow and one rise
were not laborious.
Quickness must capture errors,
as Guǒ Huái answered the Wèi Emperor,
knowing he would avoid punishment like Fáng Fēng.
Defense must withstand attack,
as Mòzǐ told the people of Chǔ,
"My disciples are already awaiting in Sòng."
Attack must overcome defense,
as Máo Suì stepped forward and said,
"Today, I follow for Chǔ,
not for Zhào."
The King of Chǔ then apologized.
Seizing must allow exchange.
Using your spear
to exchange for your shield,
leaves the owner speechless.
One who combines these eight abilities
can then comprehend the principles of the world.
Understanding the principles of the world,
one can connect with people.
If one cannot possess all eight virtues,
but only has one ability,
they are called a person of biased talent.
Then their understanding is partial,
and they are distinguished by their unique traits.
Each, based on their understanding,
establishes their name.
Thus, wisdom in discerning order through listening
is called the talent of naming things;
thought that initiates ideas
is called the talent of structuring;
insight that perceives opportunities
is called the talent of broad awareness;
eloquence that conveys intent
is called the talent of abundant provision;
quickness that captures errors
is called the talent of agility and authority;
defense that withstands attack
is called the talent of upholding arguments;
attack that overcomes defense
is called the talent of pushing through;
seizing that allows exchange
is called the talent of persuasive trade.
A person of comprehensive talent,
having all eight abilities,
practices them with the Way.
When speaking with enlightened individuals,
they share understanding and connect mind to mind;
agreement leads to mutual affirmation,
hence hearts communicate.
When speaking with the masses,
they observe expressions and adapt to natures.
If others show strong emotions,
avoid their shortcomings.
Though encompassing all principles,
they do not flaunt superiority;
always maintaining humility,
thus they stand above things.
With sharp intelligence and resources,
they do not seek to lead others;
often holding back,
thus they precede things.
Good words come from themselves,
stopping when reason is sufficient.
Once the principle is conveyed, they cease,
not indulging in verbose speech.
When others have crude errors,
they note them without pressure.
Seeing others stumble,
they promptly avoid confrontation.
They express what others harbor,
and support what others can do.
By endorsing others' abilities,
everyone takes responsibility.
