They do not use speech conventions to highlight their own strengths.
If they possess martial prowess,
they do not compare themselves to fierce tigers.
Whether speaking directly or flexibly,
they fear nothing.
The comprehensive talent calmly explains,
gaining trust before advising,
even if touching the dragon's scales,
nothing harms them.
They appreciate the good in insect sounds,
not discarding the beautiful melody
due to ugly noise.
They praise the occasional insights of fools,
not rejecting excellent words
because of the person's folly.
They seize and give appropriately,
advancing or withdrawing without hesitation.
When others are in high spirits,
they yield without regret;
not avoiding sharp falls,
nor sparing themselves from bending.
When overcoming difficulties,
they succeed without arrogance.
Reason prevails naturally,
so what is there to boast about?
With a calm heart and clear will,
without bias or rejection,
they entrust right and wrong to principle,
not craving victory for fame.
They aim only to attain the Way.
Such a person can discuss governing the world and managing affairs.
With an open and carefree mind,
they leave things to their proper place.
Thus, worldly affairs align naturally,
and all things find their order.
On Capabilities and Abilities, Part Five
Capabilities and abilities vary in scale,
their standards differ.
Assign responsibilities according to one's strength,
and the appointed tasks will be accomplished.
〈Capability〉Chapter Five
Some say:
There are talents capable of great tasks but not small ones,
just as a cauldron that can hold an ox cannot be used to cook a chicken.
I consider this a misnomer.
Talents are like vessels,
differing in size,
but using the analogy that a large cauldron cannot cook a chicken
to illustrate that great talents cannot manage small matters
is a misuse of terms.
The word "capable"
refers to an established attribute.
First, there is a fixed nature,
and then the designation of capability arises.
How can there be capability for great tasks but not for small ones?
The notion of being capable of great but not small tasks
stems from differences in temperament—some broad and some urgent.
The broad-minded are expansive and tolerant,
the urgent are intense and meticulous.
Temperaments vary in breadth and urgency,
hence suitability for different scales.
The broad-minded are fit to govern large territories,
the urgent are fit to manage small areas.
Those with broad tolerance
should administer commanderies and states,
enabling subordinates to fulfill their duties
and overseeing the completion of affairs;
whereas urgency leads to trivialities,
and tasks remain unaccomplished.
Those suited for urgent, small-scale tasks
should govern a hundred-li district,
handling affairs directly themselves.
If broad tolerance were applied, oversight would be lax,
and all matters would fall into neglect.
Thus, commanderies and counties
differ in the scale of their governance.
If one is clearly capable of governing a large commandery,
then they can govern a small commandery;
if capable of governing a large county,
they can also govern a small county.
Reasoning based on the reality of breadth and urgency,
we should say that different scales require different aptitudes,
not that one is capable of great tasks but not small ones.
If it were truly a matter of capability for great but not small tasks,
how could Confucius have declined to serve under the Jì family?
As for chickens and oxen,
they too differ in size,
but a cauldron that can cook an ox
can also cook a chicken;
while a small pot can cook a chicken,
it cannot cook a calf.
Thus, cauldrons too come in appropriate sizes.
If one is used for cooking a calf,
how could it be incapable of cooking a chicken?
It is only a matter of suitability or unsuitability,
not capability or incapability.
Therefore, if one can govern a large commandery,
they can also govern a small one.
Extending this argument,
each talent has its appropriate application,
not merely in terms of scale.
The civil-minded manage the百官 (hundred officials),
the martial-minded command the军队 (armies).
Human talents vary,
and their capabilities differ:
Some have the ability for self-reliance,
cultivating themselves and maintaining purity,
while overseeing all officials.
Some possess the ability to establish laws for others to follow,
where laws are upheld and people fear to transgress.
None dare to violate them.
Some have the ability to mediate and advocate,
using wisdom and judgment in defense,
navigating interactions with propriety.
Some have the ability to teach through virtue,
with deep understanding of the Way and methods,
their actions serving as instruction to others.
Some have the ability to conduct affairs and hold others accountable,
ensuring that words and deeds are reasonable,
and righteousness aligns with the times.
Some have the ability to inspect and rectify,
supervising right and wrong,
making clear distinctions in all matters.
Some have the ability for strategic ingenuity,
focusing on unusual tactics,
to accomplish tasks and achieve merits.
Some have the ability for awe-inspiring fierceness.
With fierce determination evident,
they intimidate enemy states.
Capability stems from one's innate material,
and materials differ in measure.
Since talents and abilities vary,
their administrative responsibilities also differ.
Thus, the ability for self-reliance
belongs to the material of pure integrity.
Therefore, in the court,
it assumes the role of the Prime Minister,
and in governing the state, it implements corrective policies.
With personal rectitude,
they thus oversee the Ministry of Heaven and manage all affairs.
The ability to establish laws
is the material of legalists.
Hence, in the court,
it holds the position of Minister of Justice,
and in state governance, it enforces impartial policies.
Laws show no favoritism,
so they manage the Ministry of Autumn and investigate crimes and violence.
The ability to devise strategies
is the material of tacticians.
Thus, in the court,
it takes on the roles of the Three Minor Ministers,
and in state affairs, it carries out adaptive policies.
With clear planning and consideration,
they assist the Three Dukes and support policy deliberation.
The ability in human affairs
is the material of insightful wisdom.
Therefore, in the court,
it serves as the assistant to the Prime Minister,
and in state governance, it implements harmonizing policies.
With careful discernment,
they aid the Ministry of Heaven in coordinating internal and external matters.
The ability in executing affairs
is the material of admonition and reprimand.
Thus, in the court,
it acts as the deputy to the Minister of Justice,
and in state affairs, it enforces supervisory policies.
Handling numerous tasks,
they assist the Ministry of Autumn in overseeing negligence.
The ability in unconventional tactics
is the material of technical skill.
Therefore, in the court,
it assumes the role of Minister of Works,
and in state governance, it manages technical affairs.
With skillful techniques,
they lead the Ministry of Winter and accomplish technical projects.
The ability in surveillance
is the material of judgment and criticism.
Thus, in the court,
it serves as the assistant to the Preceptor,
and in state affairs, it implements strict policies.
With clear distinctions between right and wrong,
they aid the Preceptor in examining good and evil.
The ability in imposing authority
is the material of heroes.
Therefore, in the court,
it takes on the role of General,
and in state governance, it enforces severe policies.
Embodied with decisiveness and resolve,
they command the six armies and project might and power.
Those with specialized talents
are like a single flavor's excellence.
For instance, malt sugar is named for its sweetness,
while wine is valued for its bitterness.
Thus they excel in managing a specific office,
like a bowyer bending wood,
with energy to spare.
But they fall short in governing a state.
If made to oversee both pottery and metalcasting,
the vessels would be ill-made.
Why is this?
The duty of a single office
uses one flavor to harmonize the five flavors.
The salt officer regulates salt,
the vinegar officer regulates vinegar,
thus the five flavors are perfected.
Like a carpenter working wood,
a mason building walls,
then great houses are completed.
The governance of a state
uses the flavorless to harmonize the five flavors.
Water, being flavorless,
allows the five flavors to achieve harmony.
Similarly, when the ruler embodies plainness,
all officials can perform their functions.
Moreover, states have different customs,
people vary in complexity and simplicity,
the five regions differ,
customs are not the same.
Soil has hardness and softness,
people have complexity and simplicity.
Since human talents differ,
governance consequently has successes and failures.
Governing simplicity with simplicity succeeds,
governing complexity with simplicity fails.
Therefore, the policy of kingly transformation
suits governing on a large scale;
simplicity brings understanding of the world's principles.
Using it for small matters
becomes impractical.
Loose nets let boat-swallowing villains escape.
The policy of meticulous supervision
suits governing complexity;
when all affairs are carefully supervised,
chaos becomes orderly.
Using it for simple matters
creates no ease.
Excessive supervision
harms the people.
The policy of strategy and tactics
suits governing difficulties;
flexible methods without fixed rules
resolve crises.
Using it in peaceful times
loses its effectiveness.
Complex techniques burden the people,
causing unrest.
The policy of strict correction
suits governing extravagance;
overcorrecting deviations
curbs wasteful luxury.
Using it for addressing shortcomings
becomes cruel.
Harsh governance of corrupt customs
harms the people.
The policy of harmony
suits governing new states;
new states have simpler rituals,
requiring temporary solutions.
Using it for established states
becomes hollow.
Temporary teachings
lack ritual substance.
The policy of impartial severity
suits rectifying wrongdoing;
without deep cutting,
villainy persists.
Using it for border regions
loses popular support.
People fearing harsh laws
easily rebel.
The policy of authority and fierceness
suits quelling rebellion;
rebellious people's defiance
requires authority to subdue.
Using it for good people
becomes tyranny.
Harsh governance harms people,
victimizing the good.
The policy of technical skill
suits governing wealth;
strengthening state and people
through management.
Using it for poverty
exhausts effort while enriching superiors and impoverishing inferiors.
Changing currency and recasting coins
deprives people of livelihood.
Thus measuring ability before appointing to office
must be carefully considered.
All such abilities
belong to those with specialized talents.
Hence some can speak but not act,
others can act but not speak.
Wisdom excels in speech,
talent excels in action.
As for those with statesman's qualities,
they can both speak and act,
thus becoming the finest among all talents.
The capability of a ruler differs from this.
He remains serene and non-interfering,
thereby entrusting tasks to the multitude of talents.
Thus, ministers consider self-reliance as their ability,
exerting themselves to achieve merits,
in order to attain ranks and positions.
The ruler regards employing people as his ability;
by appointing the worthy and utilizing the capable,
the state naturally becomes well-ordered.
Ministers view eloquent speech as their ability,
each articulating their own capabilities,
and receiving official posts accordingly.
The ruler considers attentive listening as his ability;
he listens to words and observes actions,
then assigns offices based on that.
Ministers deem effective action as their ability,
necessarily carrying out what they have professed.
The ruler sees the exercise of rewards and punishments as his ability.
These must precisely match the achievements and faults.
Their respective abilities are not the same,
with the ruler being non-active while ministers are engaged in affairs.
Hence, he can master the multitude of talents.
If the ruler were to take action himself,
replacing the master carpenter in carving,
then the various skills would lose their finesse,
and accomplishments would not be achieved.
On Benefits and Harms, Chapter Six
Establish laws and set forth strategies,
to benefit the state.
Yet when their flaws emerge,
the harm reverts to oneself.
〈Advantages and Disadvantages〉Chapter Six
For the paths of human endeavors,
each has its advantages and disadvantages.
When the flow gradually loses its source,
then advantages and disadvantages arise.
Now the path of pure virtue,
is manifested in one's demeanor,
and emanates from moral conduct.
When the mind is pure and intentions upright,
then virtuous demeanor manifests outwardly.
Even before being employed, it shines forth,
its way harmonious and transformative.
With virtuous radiance clearly displayed,
thus it proves effective without being tested.
Applying its principles to people,
therefore nothing remains un-transformed.
Thus before achieving prominence,
such a person is recommended by the multitude;
for when principles are harmonious, people gladly recommend them.
Once having achieved prominence,
such a person is respected by both superiors and subordinates.
With virtue harmonious and principles aligned,
who could possibly disrespect them?
Their merit suffices to stir up the muddy and promote the clear,
serving as model for colleagues and friends.
This as an endeavor,
remains untainted and constantly illustrious,
not merely untainted,
but existing with prominence.
Therefore it is valued by the world.
When virtue and trustworthiness are constant,
people cannot demean it.
The profession of Legalism,
is rooted in institutions,
awaiting success for its efficacy.
Laws are meant to prohibit wickedness,
and their effectiveness lies in the cessation of wickedness.
Its path is arduous at first but orderly later,
strict yet for the multitude.
Initially imposing authority,
thus it involves toil;
ultimately transforming through the Way,
thus the people are governed.
Therefore, before it is understood,
it is resented by the masses;
factions delight in chaos,
and many detest the law.
Once implemented,
it is feared by both superiors and inferiors.
Legal barriers are solemn,
causing internal and external trepidation.
Its merit suffices to establish laws and achieve order,
so the people do no wrong,
and the way of governance is realized.
Its drawback is being hated by the multitude of the crooked.
When laws favor the privileged,
they ultimately suffer harm.
As a profession, it has flaws and is not often employed,
only enlightened rulers can use it to strengthen,
but enlightenment does not span generations,
hence laws are not commonly applied.
Thus, great achievements do not endure.
Therefore, Shāng Jūn was torn apart by chariots,
Wú Qǐ dismembered.
The craft of strategists
originates from acute contemplation,
manifesting only when plans succeed.
Decided before action is taken,
people have no faith in it;
only after achievements are realized and effects proven does it become evident.
Its path begins subtle and later becomes prominent,
refined and profound.
Strategems are subtle and intricate,
their inception is supremely refined,
consistent from start to finish,
thus the Way is made manifest.
Before it is understood,
it goes unrecognized by the masses;
plans precede accomplishments,
how could the masses recognize them?
In its application,
it is treasured by enlightened rulers.
Benighted rulers, being ignorant,
how could they value it!
Its merit lies in maneuvering plans and adapting to change.
Adapting to seek success,
thus it can achieve its accomplishments.
In its retreat,
it conceals itself in obscurity.
Plans emerge from subtle secrecy,
hence they remain unrevealed.
As a profession,
it is extraordinary and rarely employed,
the master's strategies are divine and marvelous,
yet those who use them are few.
Therefore, it may sink into obscurity and not be known.
The world seldom can employ it,
how then can the Way be made manifest?
The profession of wisdom and strategy,
originates from fundamental principles,
its path is smooth and unobstructed.
Adapting to the appropriate timing,
what obstruction could there be?
Thus, before achieving success,
they are accepted by the masses;
no affairs are met with opposition,
and the virtuous draw near.
Once successful,
they are praised by those who favor them.
Harmonizing with all,
they are admired both internally and externally.
Their merit is sufficient to aid in clear planning and deliberation,
flattering and conforming to the times,
so their words and strategies are trusted.
Their downfall lies in
knowing only advancement without retreat,
failing to see jealousy and harm,
thus they crave progress.
Some deviate from righteousness to preserve themselves.
Their intentions lean toward flattery,
hence they stray from the upright path.
In their practice,
they are cunning and difficult to uphold,
concealing emotions and strategizing with cunning,
not aligned with elegance and righteousness.
Therefore, some may gain benefit first but suffer harm later.
Knowing only to advance while forgetting to retreat,
is the path to regret.
The practice of evaluation,
is rooted in judgments of right and wrong,
its path is upright and corrective.
Pure and unadulterated,
it eliminates even the slightest flaws.
Thus, before one attains recognition,
they are noticed by the masses;
pure and untainted,
they shine even in obscurity.
Once recognized,
they are praised by the multitude.
Their work is always clear and evident,
and when they emerge, they receive acclaim.
Their merit is sufficient to discern right and wrong.
With principles clear and the path pure,
right and wrong remain unconfused.
However, its drawback is
that it incurs the resentment of slanderers.
Those who slander and criticize
do not delight in hearing of their faults.
This practice is
severe and not tolerant;
being harshly observant of things,
how can it be lenient?
Thus, some may gain initial success but later become alienated from the crowd.
Clarity and integrity are praised by the times,
while harsh principles are feared by the masses.
The craft of skill and artifice,
originates from practical abilities,
its way is discerning and swift.
Skillful strategies are divine-like,
hence the rapid discernment.
Before one attains understanding,
they are regarded as different by the masses;
with abilities standing out from the crowd,
thus even if subtle, they become evident.
Once understanding is reached,
they are entrusted by officials.
Accomplishing tasks and achieving success,
is what governance strives for.
Their merit is sufficient to manage troubles and correct wrongs.
Resolving complexities and rectifying evils,
also requires skill and artifice.
Its drawback, however,
is that the people toil and the lower ranks suffer.
When those above have many demands, those below are distressed.
As a profession,
it is meticulous but not grand,
thus it is the lesser aspect of governance.
If the way is not broad and expansive,
how can it achieve greatness?
Chapter Seven: On Connecting with Recognitions
Extending from oneself to interact with others,
all recognize the same essence.
A person of versatile abilities
can then comprehend the multitude of talents.
"On Recognizing Others" Part Seven
People are initially very difficult to understand,
with their sincere appearances and deep emotions,
making them hard to truly know.
Yet scholars, regardless of their number,
all believe they can understand others.
Thus, judging others by oneself,
they think it's possible to know them;
if one values integrity,
then all who are upright are considered within one's understanding.
Observing how others perceive people,
they assume those others do not recognize true character.
Why is that?
Because what one values oneself
lies in integrity;
while what others favor
is profit and desire.
When right and wrong differ from theirs,
they claim others fail to discern true worth.
Therefore, one can recognize the virtues of those similar,
such as those skilled in strategy due to their thoughtful nature.
But may overlook the beauty in those of different capacities.
Though adherents to law have their merits,
strategists do not value them.
How to explain this?
Those of integrity
use uprightness as their standard,
so when assessing various talents,
they can recognize consistent moral conduct,
and with uprightness as their measure,
they appreciate steadfast individuals.
But may doubt the cunning of legal tactics,
believing upholding righteousness suffices for governance—
why resort to methods and schemes?
Legalists
use rules and divisions as their standard,
so they can gauge the capacity for fairness,
and with legal divisions as their measure,
they value straightforward people.
But do not esteem the art of adaptability,
thinking rules and divisions are enough to achieve success—
why need strategic planning?
Strategists
use deep thought as their standard,
so they can appreciate the wonders of tactics,
and with strategy as their measure,
they prize tactical minds.
But fail to see the goodness in following laws,
believing strategic thought can transform the people—
why rely on legal systems?
Those with practical ability
use defense and debate as their standard,
so they recognize the principles of planning,
and with debate as their measure,
they admire those with strategic plans.
But do not understand the roots of institutions,
thinking strategies are sufficient to achieve merits—
why need established systems?
The insightful
use tracing intentions as their standard,
so they grasp the subtleties of hidden schemes,
and with intent-tracing as their measure,
they favor those with covert plans.
But do not value the constancy of laws and teachings,
believing that understanding intentions is enough for correctness—
why bother with legal principles?
The crafty
use seeking merit as their standard,
so they recognize the achievements of advancement,
and with merit-seeking as their measure,
they appreciate those with functional skills.
But do not comprehend the transformation of morality,
thinking that skill is enough to accomplish tasks—
why care for moral virtue?
The critical
use scrutiny as their standard,
so they discern the clarity in reproof,
and with scrutiny as their measure,
they like those who censure.
But do not appreciate unconventional uniqueness,
believing that criticism completes education—
why embrace broad-mindedness?
The eloquent
use analysis as their standard,
so they perceive the quickness in wit,
and with dissection as their measure,
they admire the sharp-tongued.
But do not recognize the beauty of reserved elegance,
thinking debate clarifies matters—
why value subtlety?
Thus they refute each other,
and none is willing to affirm the other.
Everyone considers themselves to be right,
so who would acknowledge others' correctness?
When sharing the same nature,
they connect harmoniously and find mutual accord;
if their innate qualities align,
then even as distantly as Hú and Yuè,
they resonate and communicate in spirit.
When possessing different natures,
they remain unfamiliar despite long acquaintance.
If their innate qualities differ,
then even shoulder-to-shoulder neighbors,
grow more distant with each passing year.
All cases of this kind
refer to individuals of the same category of talent.
Therefore, same nature brings closeness,
while different natures create distance.
If possessing two or more attributes,
they also follow what they combine
to extend to different measures.
Legalists incorporate methods,
thus able to use methods to support laws.
Hence, single-category individuals
can recognize the excellence of their own category;
those who govern by law
promote nothing beyond the law.
Dual-category individuals
can appreciate the virtues of both categories.
Those embodying law and method
implement both law and method simultaneously.
When encompassing all categories,
they can comprehensively understand all talents.
One who embodies all eight categories
positions the eight talents appropriately,
leaving no matter unmanaged.
Therefore, multifaceted talent individuals align with the state's structure.
This means eight-talented individuals,
when first advancing present their proposals.
The office of the Zhǒngzǎi
examines their rationale.
To observe but a corner of it,
a single morning suffices to know it.
To delve into its details,
then three days are required.
Why say three days are required?
Because a person embodying the state's essence combines three talents,
thus a discussion not lasting three days is insufficient to exhaust them.
First, to discuss the Way and virtue,
second, to discuss laws and institutions,
third, to discuss strategies and methods,
only then can one fully draw out their strengths and recommend them without doubt.
Those in high positions who comprehend all eight talents
can then fully utilize those they advance and employ without hesitation.
So how can one discern whether a person is comprehensive or one-sided and engage in conversation accordingly?
When observing someone's speech, how can one identify a one-sided talent,
and how can one recognize a comprehensive talent?
If a person
strives to categorize others' strengths through various schools of thought and assign them labels,
this indicates comprehensiveness.
Whenever they exhaustively classify others' capabilities based on types of affairs and assign names,
they speak incessantly.
When presenting virtues,
they desire others' praise.
If they boast of their own goodness by relating it to events,
and further wish others to constantly speak well of them,
yet show no interest in understanding others' qualities—this indicates one-sidedness.
When others possess virtues,
their ears dislike hearing of them;
when others are praised,
their mouths do not join in agreement.
Unwilling to understand others,
they inevitably doubt every word.
Hearing of strict laws, they suspect harshness;
hearing of strategies, they suspect deceit.
Thus, explaining profound ideas to a shallow mind
only deepens the divergence.
The shallow-minded think narrowly,
so upon hearing profound principles, their hearts grow more perplexed.
Hence, when Shāng Jūn expounded the Way of Emperors and Kings without success,
he showed them the principles of strengthening the military instead.
Divergence leads to opposition,
opposition leads to mutual rejection.
Hearing profundity, the heart becomes confused—
how could there be mutual agreement?
Thus, Lǐ Duì plugged his ears and refused to listen to Sū Qín's persuasions.
Therefore, presenting many straightforward arguments
is seen as showing off;
due to their multifaceted nature,
they are suspected of flaunting.
Listening quietly without speaking
is taken as emptiness;
waiting for the right moment to speak,
they are suspected of having no substance.
Engaging in lofty discourse
is viewed as arrogance;
with guarded words and high reasoning,
they are suspected of belittling others.
Being modest and reserved
is considered shallow;
with humble speech and little vigor,
they are suspected of superficiality.
Mentioning a single virtue
is seen as lacking breadth;
not daring to elaborate much,
they are suspected of narrow-mindedness.
Enumerating many wonders
is taken as being scattered;
widely citing examples of affairs,
intending to explain thoroughly,
is again seen as being scattered.
Speaking ahead of others' intentions
is viewed as stealing their glory;
if words match their thoughts,
they suspect you of taking credit.
Pointing out faults through questioning
is taken as incomprehension;
trying to correct their mistakes,
you are instead seen as ignorant.
Using opposing arguments in discussion
is viewed as competing;
wanting to refute matters and speak plainly,
you are suspected of rivalry.
Expressing diverse and varied knowledge
is considered lacking focus;
pouring out all one's thoughts
is called aimlessness.
Only when discussing with like-minded individuals
does one then feel pleased.
When brothers quarrel fiercely,
and the story of Guǎn Shū and Cài Shū is recounted,
they become cheerful and harmonious.
Thus, feelings of affection arise,
along with praises and recommendations.
If words align,
it is not merely affection,
but even leading to praise and promotion.
These are the common flaws of one-sided talents.
Their minds often cling stubbornly,
wanting others to agree with them,
yet they themselves do not necessarily attain it—
how could they temporarily achieve it?
Chapter Eight: On Heroes
If not for their extraordinary nature,
how could each have gained renown?
The "Yīng" represents literary brilliance,
the "Xióng" signifies martial fame.
"Heroes" Chapter Eight
Among plants, the most exquisite and splendid are called yīng; among beasts, the exceptionally outstanding are called xióng.
If even things possess this distinction,
how much more so for humans!
Therefore, when humans excel exceptionally in civil or martial virtues,
they derive their names from this.
The civil takes yīng as its name,
the martial takes xióng as its title.
Hence, those with outstanding intelligence and brilliance are called yīng,
those with surpassing courage and strength are called xióng,
this is the general distinction in their designations.
If we compare their components,
they mutually depend on each other.
Yīng must possess a portion of xióng,
then it can achieve refinement;
Xiong must possess a portion of yīng,
then it can achieve firmness.
Each with its two parts,
takes one part from the other,
only then is completion achieved.
Courage is the component of xióng,
wisdom is the component of yīng.
Yīng has intelligence,
but requires courage to be realized;
Xiong has courage and strength,
but requires wisdom to be established.
How can we argue this to be so?
For intelligence and acuity,
are the attributes of the "Yīng" (the brilliant strategist),
but without the courage of the "Xióng" (the valiant warrior),
then their proposals cannot be implemented;
wisdom without courage
cannot uphold righteous speech.
Courage and strength,
are the attributes of the "Xióng",
but without the wisdom of the "Yīng",
then affairs cannot be established.
Bravery without strategy
cannot accomplish tasks.
Therefore, the "Yīng" uses their intelligence to plan the beginning,
and their acuity to perceive opportunities,
wisdom to strategize the initiation of affairs,
acuity to discern the pivotal moments.
They await the courage of the "Xióng" to act;
without resolution, action is impossible.
The "Xióng" uses their strength to subdue the masses,
and their bravery to overcome difficulties,
without strength, the masses will not submit,
without bravery, difficulties cannot be overcome.
They await the wisdom of the "Yīng" to achieve success.
Wisdom adapts to circumstances,
thus skill can accomplish goals.
Only then can each fulfill their strengths.
Just as metal relies on water to achieve sharpness and function,
things obtain water to then achieve nurturing effects.
If one has the intelligence to plan the beginning,
but lacks the acuity to perceive opportunities,
they may be fit for seated discussions,
but not for handling affairs;
though wise enough for seated discussions,
if acuity fails to see opportunities,
how can they manage any affairs?
If one has the intelligence to plan the beginning,
and the acuity to perceive opportunities,
but lacks the bravery to act,
they can follow routines,
but cannot contemplate changes.
Though capable of following routines,
if bravery is absent for action,
how can they respond to changes?
If one has strength surpassing others,
but lacks the bravery to act,
they may be a strong person,
but not fit to be a vanguard;
even if peerless in strength,
if courage is indecisive,
how can they serve as a vanguard?
If one has strength surpassing others,
and bravery to act,
but lacks the wisdom to make decisions,
they may serve as a vanguard,
but are insufficient to be a general.
Though strong enough to lead the charge,
if they face affairs without strategy,
how can they function as a general?
One must have the intelligence to plan the beginning,
the acuity to perceive opportunities,
and the courage to make decisions,
only then can they be considered "Yīng",
as exemplified by Zhāng Liáng;
with physical strength surpassing others,
bravery to act,
and wisdom sufficient to decide matters,
only then can they be considered "Xióng",
as exemplified by Hán Xìn.
Their inherent attributes differ,
and they are categorized based on their predominance,
hence the distinct names "Yīng" and "Xióng".
Zhāng Liáng had more of the "Yīng's" wisdom,
Hán Xìn excelled in the "Xióng's" courage.
Yet both were talents of partial excellence,
suited for the roles of ministers.
Thus, the "Yīng" can serve as chancellor,
achieving victory in court.
The "Xióng" can serve as general,
spreading awe afar.
If one person's character
combines both "Yīng" and "Xióng",
then they can rule for generations,
as exemplified by Gāozǔ and Xiàng Yǔ.
Yet the measure of refinement must exceed that of prowess,
and refinement cannot be lacking.
Refinement brings forth wisdom,
and wisdom can command prowess—
how could it be dispensable?
If the measure of refinement is small,
then the wise will depart.
Thus, Xiàng Yǔ, whose strength overshadowed the age,
whose clarity adapted to change,
whose courage knew no fear,
and who crossed the river and burned provisions,
yet could not listen to or adopt extraordinary counsel,
possessed a Fàn Zēng but did not employ him,
so that those like Chén Píng all fled and returned to Gāozǔ.
His measure of refinement was great,
thus the multitude of powerful leaders submitted to him,
and the talented and refined returned to him,
both finding their use.
Once the powerful were subdued,
the refined also came to him.
Therefore, he could swallow Qín and crush Chǔ,
dwelling as master of all under heaven.
Thus, the proportion of refinement and prowess
is the measure of self-mastery.
Victory lies within oneself,
then one can overcome external things.
If one has only refinement without prowess,
then the powerful will not submit;
with no master within,
how can external things enter?
If one has only prowess without refinement,
then the wise will not come;
with no means to connect with them,
how would the wise have a way to come?
Thus, prowess can attract the powerful,
but cannot attract the refined;
rhinoceros and tigers naturally form their own groups.
Refinement can attract the refined,
but cannot attract the powerful;
luan birds and phoenixes naturally draw close to each other.
Therefore, only when one person’s nature
combines both refinement and prowess
can they command both the refined and the powerful.
Being able to command both the refined and the powerful,
they can thus accomplish great deeds.
Using force to subdue them,
and culture to pacify them,
then achievements will flourish in their time,
and blessings will flow to later generations.
The Ninth Chapter: Eight Observations
Various talents differ in kind,
Their aspirations diverge in direction.
Observe whether they connect or not,
The criteria are eight in total.
"Eight Observations" Chapter Nine
The eight observations are:
First, observe their deprivations and rescues,
to clarify inconsistencies;
some may wish to be compassionate and aid others but are hindered by stinginess from practicing benevolence,
others may broadly and generously provide relief yet beg for vinegar as a favor.
Second, observe their reactions to changes,
to discern their constant norms;
by watching their expressions of anger or shame,
their constant norms can be discerned.
Third, observe their essential qualities,
to understand their reputation;
when inner qualities correspond outwardly,
one can discern their name by observing their demeanor.
Fourth, observe their motives,
to distinguish between imitation and genuineness;
imitative criticism may seem straightforward,
but in haste, it is hard to clarify.
Examine what they are at ease with,
and it becomes clearly distinguishable.
Fifth, observe their love and respect,
to understand connection or obstruction;
pure love fosters closeness and emotional connection,
while pure respect leads to distance and emotional blockage.
Sixth, observe their emotional triggers,
to discern forgiveness or confusion;
when their desires are met, they are forgiving,
when their desires are thwarted, they are confused.
Seventh, observe their shortcomings,
to know their strengths;
though criticism and fault-finding are shortcomings,
they excel in upholding integrity.
Eighth, observe their intelligence,
to know what they can achieve.
Even if one possesses many talents,
but lacks intelligence,
everything will be obscured and blocked,
how could they possibly achieve anything?
What is meant by observing what is overridden and what is preserved to understand mixed traits?
Human nature encompasses both the ultimate and the deviant.
An unyielding nature free from desires
represents the ultimate;
while greed and emotions prevailing
signify the deviant.
If the ultimate overcomes the deviant,
then evil emotions override righteousness,
appearing so but not truly so.
When desires overcome unyieldingness,
it seems unyielding yet is not.
Thus, benevolence stems from compassion,
yet some are compassionate but not benevolent;
benevolence must involve relief,
yet some are benevolent but offer no relief;
severity must entail firmness,
yet some are severe but not firm.
For instance, upon seeing pitiable situations, one may shed tears,
with compassion arising from within.
But when it comes to sharing, they become stingy—
this is being compassionate without benevolence.
A benevolent person must provide relief.
Witnessing danger and urgency, one feels sympathy,
with benevolent feelings stirred inside.
Yet when rushing to help, they fear harm—
this is being benevolent without offering relief.
One who provides relief must brave dangers.
In discussing empty righteousness, one appears stern,
with intensity showing in demeanor.
But facing profit and desires, they weaken internally—
this is being severe without firmness.
A firm person must be free from desires.
Therefore, those compassionate but not benevolent
have their compassion overridden by stinginess;
loving wealth harms compassion.
Those benevolent but not relieving
have their benevolence overridden by fear;
timidity damages benevolence.
Those severe but not firm
have their severity overridden by desires;
profit and desires harm firmness.
Hence it is said:
If compassion cannot overcome stinginess,
one cannot be assured of benevolence;
if love does not lead to giving,
how can benevolence be achieved?
If benevolence cannot overcome fear,
one cannot be assured of relief;
if fear and cowardice prevent action,
how can relief be carried out?
If severity cannot overcome desires,
one cannot be assured of firmness;
if the heart dwells on profit and desires,
how can firmness be attained?
Thus, if an unbenevolent nature prevails,
then skills and strength become tools of harm;
if a benevolent nature is weak yet one possesses skills,
these become instruments of self-destruction.
If a greedy and rebellious nature triumphs,
then strength and fierceness become steps to disaster;
if integrity is lacking and the nature is strong and fierce,
this becomes a ladder to one's own ruin.
There are also cases where good emotions save evil,
not leading to harm;
though evil should be cut off and eliminated,
a purely good person pities and saves it—
such a deeply kind person
poses no great harm.
With deep and sincere affection and generosity,
even arrogance and familiarity do not lead to separation.
In lifelong friendships,
with deep emotions and strong bonds,
even if one acts as disrespectfully as Yuǎn Rǎng, they are not abandoned—
there is no major fault.
If aiding goodness is prominent,
even harboring hatred toward evil
does no harm;
such as eliminating the unprincipled to uphold the principled,
no matter how intense the hatred,
there is no great wrong.
If relief and aid are excessively generous,
even taking from others
is not greed;
taking others' possessions to provide relief,
even if criticized for begging for vinegar,
is not major greed.
Therefore, by observing what is overridden and what is preserved,
the nature of mixed traits can be understood.
Some have compassion and benevolence overridden by fear or stinginess,
some provide relief beyond their means,
yet a balanced ruler accommodates and forgives.
What does it mean to observe their reactions,
in order to examine their constant disposition?
People have deep-seated emotions behind thick appearances,
and if one wishes to seek them out,
one must observe the intent of their words,
and examine their responses and agreements.
Look at the main point of their speech,
and observe whether their echoes and agreements are appropriate.
Observing the intent of their words
is like discerning the quality of a sound;
when a sound is produced, its quality is distinguished.
Examining their responses and agreements
is like assessing the capacity of their wisdom.
When voices harmonize, their capabilities are distinguished.
Therefore, by observing words and examining responses,
one can sufficiently distinguish and recognize each other.
One sings, the other harmonizes,
right and wrong are mutually raised.
Thus, when arguments reveal and uphold correctness,
it is clarity;
when words are evident and advocacy is upright,
this is called clear understanding.
Poor at verbal response,
it is obscurity;
silently recognizing it,
this is called profundity.
Weaving together the profound and the clear,
it is comprehension;
clearly distinguishing right from wrong,
can be termed understanding principles.
Shifting without constancy,
it is confusion;
principles not consistently upheld,
words and meanings are muddled and mixed.
Foreseeing what has not yet occurred,
is sageliness;
reflecting on profound matters,
is acuity;
understanding affairs beyond others,
is insight;
using insight to appear obscure,
is wisdom;
though the mind understands,
it always seems insufficient.
Detecting the subtlest details,
is marvel;
though principles are extremely subtle,
one can perceive them.
Exquisite and unobscured,
is lucidity;
the mind achieves clarity,
this is called transparent brightness.
The deeper one probes, the more substantial it is;
it is genuineness;
the mind possesses solid wisdom,
the more one explores, the more refined it becomes,
like a spring bubbling up from within,
the deeper one probes, the more profound it is.
Falsely assembled and showy,
it is emptiness;
hearsay and rumor,
over time lack substance,
like a pond without a source,
draining away to emptiness and exhaustion.
Displaying one's own beauty,
is insufficiency;
wisdom not fully sufficient,
fears others' ignorance and thus boasts.
Not boasting of one's ability,
is abundance;
not fearing being unknown.
Therefore it is said:
In all affairs, if they are not measured,
there must be a reason.
If facial expressions lose authenticity,
there must be a cause of worry or joy.
The countenance of distress,
is weary and haggard;
with worry in the heart,
thus the appearance becomes haggard.
The look of illness,
is disordered and grimy in texture.
Yellow and black colors mixed,
the skin texture is dusty and dirty.
A joyful expression is pleasantly cheerful,
an angry expression is stern and heightened.
The look of jealousy and confusion,
is reckless and inconsistent,
alternately pale and red,
agitatedly visible on the face.
And when it comes to their actions,
they are generally accompanied by speech.
Once the expression is animated,
words follow accordingly.
Therefore, if one's words are very cheerful,
but the essence of their expression does not follow,
there is internal conflict;
the heart resents while the words force harmony,
the expression and appearance ultimately do not align.
If the words are contradictory,
but the essence of the expression is trustworthy,
it is due to inarticulateness.
Words do not fully express themselves,
so although the speech contradicts, the expression remains credible.
If an angry look appears before words are spoken,
it means indignation is overflowing;
for those filled with rage in the chest,
the expression shows before any words are uttered.
If anger accompanies the words after they are spoken,
it is forcing what is not so.
Wanting to强行 enforce what is not right,
hence anger aids the speech.
All such types,
manifest outwardly as signs,
and cannot be concealed or contradicted.
The heart is joyful but the face shows anger,
the mind resents but the appearance is harmonious.
Even if one wishes to contradict it,
the essence of the expression does not comply.
When the heart is moved, the appearance follows.
Reactions and astonishments make it clear,
even through changes, they can be known.
Though emotions are internal,
reactions and astonishments emerge externally.
With countless forms and appearances,
they can be roughly understood.
Therefore, by observing their reactions,
the nature of their constant disposition can be known.
By observing a person's words and expressions, one can know their heart,
things have constant measures,
and then they can be carefully examined.
What is meant by observing one's fundamental substance to understand their reputation?
In the nature of those with partial talents,
when two excellences are present or more,
then the supreme qualities interact,
giving rise to a commendable reputation.
The two excellences
refer to substance and vitality.
When substance is upright and vitality pure,
a good reputation is born.
Thus, with bones straight and vitality clear,
an excellent reputation emerges;
when bone structure and vitality correspond,
the reputation is thereby beautiful.
With pure vitality and strong strength,
a fierce reputation arises;
since vitality is already pure,
strength makes it fierce.
With sharp intellect and refined principles,
a capable reputation is born;
since intellect is already sharp,
refined principles bring capability.
With straightforward intelligence and strong sincerity,
a trustworthy reputation emerges.
Being both upright and excellent,
thus one is entrusted.
When gathered in upright substance,
virtuous character is achieved;
when substance manifests harmony and integrity,
good virtue is then formed.
Adding learning to this,
then literary pattern shines forth.
Though jade has substance,
polishing reveals its pattern.
Therefore, by observing how many excellences one possesses,
the different types of reputation that arise can be known.
By examining their substance and vitality,
observing their purity and turbidity,
although there may be differences in degree,
and names for different conditions,
they can definitely be discerned.
What is meant by observing one's motives
to distinguish between imitation and resemblance?
Pure fault-finding violates human nature,
incapable of impartiality;
when both substance and temperament are given to censure,
what rectitude can there be?
Imitating censure resembles integrity,
using censure to expose goodness;
employing censure under the guise of integrity,
censure extends to the virtuous and good.
Pure frivolity resembles adaptability,
incapable of comprehending the Way;
when both substance and temperament are frivolous,
what Way can be comprehended?
Imitating frivolity resembles comprehension,
acting arrogantly beyond measure.
Frivolity masquerading as comprehension,
indulges arrogance without restraint.
Therefore it is said:
The straightforward also censure,
the censorious also censure;
their censure is the same,
but their reasons for censuring differ.
The censure of straightforward people
condemns evil and fears wrongdoing;
pure censure for its own sake
attacks goodness and criticizes what is right.
The adaptable also act frivolously,
the frivolous also act frivolously;
their frivolity is the same,
but their reasons for being frivolous differ.
The frivolity of adaptable people
is simple and attains the Way.
Pure frivolity is arrogantly eccentric and self-indulgent.
How then can they be distinguished?
Straightforward yet capable of gentleness
constitutes virtue;
gentleness combined with straightforwardness
is what constitutes virtue.
Straightforward yet fond of censuring
is partiality;
a straightforward nature excessively given to censure
constitutes partiality.
Censorious yet not straightforward
is imitation.
Pure censure resembling straightforwardness
constitutes imitation.
Following the Way yet capable of restraint
is comprehension;
restraining oneself through the Way
constitutes comprehension.
Comprehensive yet occasionally excessive
is partiality;
a comprehensive nature occasionally excessive
constitutes partiality.
Frivolous without restraint
is imitation.
Pure frivolity resembling comprehension
constitutes imitation.
Partiality and imitation
share aspirations but differ in substance,
which is what is called seeming right but actually wrong.
Substance identical to comprehension and straightforwardness
may be partial or imitative.
Therefore, lightly making promises resembles fervor but lacks trustworthiness;
not measuring one's own strength,
lightly pledging to die for others,
yet fearing danger when crisis comes,
unable to sacrifice one's life.
Taking many things lightly resembles capability but yields no results;
disregarding one's abilities,
claiming one can handle affairs,
yet acting recklessly when undertaking tasks,
producing no effective outcomes.
Rapid advancement resembles excellence but soon departs;
impetuous individuals
cannot endure long.
Nitpicking resembles scrutiny but complicates matters;
those given to fault-finding
often create much confusion.
Censorious generosity resembles kindness but accomplishes nothing;
momentarily appearing sufficient,
ultimately achieving nothing.
Surface compliance resembles loyalty but contradicts in private;
obsequious agreement in the moment,
yet self-willed when withdrawn.
These are cases of seeming right but actually wrong.
Purple confuses vermilion,
which the sage detests.
There are also cases of seeming wrong but actually right:
actions similar to wrong,
yet their merit is actually right.
Great authority resembles treachery but achieves merit;
Yǐ Fú exiled Tài Jiǎ,
thereby accomplishing his merit.
Great wisdom resembles foolishness but is inwardly perceptive;
all day not opposing,
yet inwardly truly discerning.
Universal love seems empty but is actually profound;
loving all without selfishness,
seems empty but is real.
Upright speech seems censorious but is sincerely loyal.
Criticizing emperors like Jié and Zhòu,
with utmost sincerity and loyal devotion.
To discern semblances and clarify errors,
mastering the reversals of human feelings,
wishing to examine similar types,
scrutinizing principles to distinguish right from wrong,
mastering and capturing human sentiments,
repeatedly clarifying them.
It resembles adjudicating disputes,
but is actually difficult to distinguish.
Therefore, the sage consults widely and inquires extensively,
sharing with the multitude.
Without the utmost refinement under heaven,
who can grasp the reality?
If the reality could be obtained,
why worry about Huān Dōu?
Why banish the Yǒu Miáo?
Thus, rising early at dawn,
illuminating the obscure and humble,
speaking with the Three Locusts,
inquiring of the Nine Thorns.
So, trusting speech and appearance
may miss the truth;
awkward speech and plain appearance—
Zhòngní missed it with Zǐ Yǔ.
Deceptive feelings mastering reversals,
may miss the worthy;
doubting what seems inhuman—
Gōngsūn missed it with Bǔ Shì.
The discernment of worthiness and unworthiness
truly lies in what is relied upon.
Although difficult to know,
one should seek what is relied upon and examine it.
Therefore, by observing what one relies upon,
the substance of semblances can be known.
Although not fully grasping the reality,
by examining what is relied upon and resembled,
then one's physical and temperamental substance
can roughly be approximated.
What is meant by observing one's love and respect to understand communication and obstruction?
For the ultimate principle of human relations
is nothing beyond love and respect.
Love originates between father and son,
while respect is established between ruler and minister.
Therefore, the Classic of Filial Piety regards love as the supreme virtue,
which initiates the intimacy between father and son,
thus being the supreme virtue.
It considers respect as the essential way;
completing the righteousness between ruler and minister,
thus being the core of the Way.
The Book of Changes takes influence as virtue,
where vital energy connects and generates things,
enabling humans to benefit from nourishment.
It regards humility as the Way;
distinctions between noble and humble
create the order of the Way.
Laozi considers non-action as virtue,
exercising transformation without fixed methods,
which is the principle of virtue.
He takes emptiness as the Way.
Tranquil and non-acting,
this is the nature of the Way.
Ritual takes respect as its foundation,
as ritual arises from the yin principle,
solemn and pure.
Music takes love as its essence.
Since music comes from the yang principle,
it brings joyful affection.
Thus, in the substance of human nature,
there exists the sincerity of love and respect.
Even during infancy,
love and respect begin to emerge.
Then they share the same substance with morality,
moving and winning people's hearts,
so the Way becomes unimpeded.
Embracing the Way and cultivating virtue,
thus matters follow principle and communication flows.
However, love cannot be less than respect.
If love is less than respect,
then the incorruptible and disciplined will adhere,
as upright people value respect,
hence they adhere.
But the masses will not follow;
since ordinary people delight in love,
if love is insufficient,
they will not follow.
If love exceeds respect,
then even the incorruptible may be displeased,
yet those connected by love will die for it.
Incorruptible people are few,
while ordinary people are many.
When the masses delight in love to the point of dying for it,
then affairs succeed and enterprises prosper.
Therefore, the way of love
cannot be insufficient.
Why is this?
Because the way of respect
is strict and creates distance,
making it difficult to sustain;
every action requires solemn demeanor,
which cannot be maintained long.
Travelers at an inn
do not stay until warmth is offered before departing.
The way of love,
with deep affection and profound care,
penetrates and moves people deeply.
Warm and sincere intimacy
moves people profoundly - extremely deeply.
Thus, the man at Yìsāng
turned his spear to repay virtue.
Therefore, by observing the sincerity of one's love and respect,
the principles of communication and obstruction can be known.
Being profound in compassionate love
brings warmth and connects the feelings between superiors and subordinates;
focusing on ritual respect
creates solemnity but blocks internal and external feelings.
However, love and respect must complement each other,
neither can be absent at any time.
Yet in practicing these two principles,
one should always ensure that love exceeds respect,
then the atmosphere of solemn reverence can be nearly achieved.
What is meant by observing their emotional triggers,
to distinguish between tolerance and confusion?
Human emotions have six triggers:
When their desires are fulfilled, they rejoice;
praising Wūhuò to those with strength,
their hearts are invariably delighted.
When their abilities are not utilized, they resent;
commending Sānjiān to the eloquent,
their hearts are invariably indignant.
When others boast and surpass them, they dislike it;
flaunting one's own capabilities,
to outshine the crowd,
is what people detest.
When approached with humility and deference, they are pleased;
humbling oneself beneath others,
makes everyone joyful.
When their shortcomings are confronted, they become hostile;
people all delight in their own strengths,
and dislike their own weaknesses,
so highlighting their shortcomings
leads to hostility and outbursts of anger.
When disliked actions provoke hostility, it breeds jealousy.
Boasting of one's abilities,
is what others dislike;
pointing out others' weaknesses,
is what others resent.
Now, flaunting one's capabilities
and provoking others' resentments
gives rise to envy and harm.
These are the six triggers of human emotions.
Human nature invariably seeks to fulfill its aspirations,
what the will desires,
is to see them realized and accomplished.
Thus, the resolute delight in the achievements of exerted strength;
when difficulties arise, the strong strive.
The virtuous delight in the guidance of overseeing governance;
when governance is cultivated, the virtuous are employed.
The capable delight in managing affairs of order and chaos;
amid order and chaos, the worthy and able are sought.
The strategic delight in devising plans and schemes;
broad calculations seek their strategies.
The eloquent delight in soaring rhetoric and inquiries;
hosting and assisting seek their articulate contributions.
The greedy delight in accumulating goods and wealth;
when wealth is amassed,
the greedy find their desires accommodated.
The favored delight in exceptional power and influence.
When power and influence are exceptional,
the favored seize their control.
If their aspirations are affirmed,
none fail to be joyful.
This is what is called fulfilling their desires,
then they rejoice;
when the heart's desires are fully met,
what resentment remains?
If their abilities are not utilized,
their aspirations are not attained,
and if aspirations are not attained,
they grieve.
Worrying that their talents go unexpressed.
Hence, if achievements and efforts are not established,
the resolute strive;
striving,
from frustration at not fully employing their abilities.
If moral conduct is not cultivated,
the upright mourn;
mourning,
saddened that their transformative influence cannot be implemented.
If governance is chaotic and unmanaged,
the capable sigh;
sighing,
lamenting that their capabilities cannot be applied.
If enemies' capabilities are not quelled,
the strategists ponder;
pondering,
thinking that their ingenious plans cannot be deployed.
If goods and wealth are not accumulated,
the greedy worry;
worrying,
concerned that there is no gain to be reaped.
If power and influence are not exceptional,
the favored lament.
Lamenting,
saddened that they cannot manipulate authority.
This is what is called not utilizing their abilities,
then they resent.
The resentment lies in not utilizing their abilities, which would bring joy.
Human nature invariably seeks to be ahead,
thus disliking others' self-promotion.
All wish to precede others,
hence resenting others' self-aggrandizement.
Self-promotion,
is of the kind that all desire to surpass.
Therefore, boasting of one's virtues,
is universally disliked.
Disliking the intention to surpass oneself.
This is what is called self-promotion that surpasses others,
then it is disliked.
Thus, the enlightened never boast of themselves.
Human nature seeks victory,
thus rejoicing in others' humility.
Humility serves to lower oneself,
implying deference and concession.
Therefore, regardless of worthiness or folly,
if approached with humility,
all will show pleased expressions.
Regardless of capability,
all wish to surpass others.
This is what is called approaching with humility,
then they are pleased.
Thus, the noble person remains humble all day long.
Human nature seeks to conceal shortcomings,
and display strengths.
Praising their strengths pleases them,
while mentioning their shortcomings angers them.
Thus, when others criticize their weaknesses,
it feels as if something is imposed upon them.
The emotion of frustration and suppression,
is like being overwhelmed.
This is what is called confronting their deficiencies,
then they become hostile.
Overwhelmed and obstructed,
their hearts turn hostile and defiant.
Human nature tends to surpass superiors.
Seeing others excel themselves,
all wish to outdo them.
Encroaching upon what they dislike,
though it may cause animosity,
does not necessarily bring harm.
Though they dislike my self-promotion,
it is not severely harmful.
But if using strengths to criticize weaknesses,
this is what is called provoking hostility with disliked actions,
then jealousy arises.
Using one's own strengths
to attack others' weaknesses,
inviting harm,
is why the enlightened avoid it.
All these six triggers,
ultimately stem from the desire to be superior.
The inherent arrogance of things,
is universal among people.
Therefore, the noble person in interactions,
endures offenses without retaliation.
Knowing that emotions tend toward competitiveness,
even if others slightly offend them,
they ultimately do not resist or retaliate.
Not retaliating,
then all are respected and deferred to,
thus avoiding harm.
Diligently practicing humility and respect,
who would harm them?
Petty individuals are not so;
they fail to perceive the mechanisms,
not understanding the triggers of jealousy and harm.
Yet they desire others to comply with them,
meaning they want no opposition.
They mistake feigned affection and respect as special treatment;
like Kǒng Guāng's hesitation,
Dǒng Xián's delight.
They take occasional invitations as slights;
deeming them insincere,
they resent the perceived disrespect.
If their triggers are provoked,
they deeply hold grudges.
Petty people are easily pleased but difficult to serve.
Thus, by observing their emotional triggers,
the intentions of the worthy and base can be discerned.
The worthy and enlightened aim to defer,
the base and inferior aim to surpass.
Therefore, the impartial ruler,
governs with correctness,
instructing the greedy on their worries,
admonishing the favored on their sorrows.
Then, none boast of themselves,
inferiors do not surpass superiors,
the worthy and unworthy hold appropriate positions,
and the path of governance follows order.
What does it mean to observe a person's shortcomings to know their strengths?
People with one-sided talents
all have their shortcomings.
Their wisdom cannot be comprehensive.
Thus the flaw of straightforwardness is harsh criticism,
as harsh criticism violates righteousness,
hence when a father stole a sheep,
his son bore witness against him.
The flaw of firmness is severity,
as rigid adherence injures reason,
so when advising the ruler was unheeded,
one resorted to the sword.
The flaw of gentleness is timidity,
as timidity falls short of the Way,
thus Gōng Zhīqí, being timid,
could not remonstrate forcefully.
The flaw of integrity is inflexibility.
Inflexible simplicity fails in practical matters,
as Wěi Shēng, keeping his word,
died beneath the bridge.
If the straightforward do not criticize harshly,
they cannot achieve their straightforwardness;
since one appreciates their straightforwardness,
one cannot condemn their harsh criticism.
To employ a person's straightforwardness,
tolerate their harsh criticism.
Harsh criticism
is the mark of straightforwardness.
Without harsh criticism, one cannot be straightforward.
If the firm are not severe,
they cannot sustain their firmness;
since one appreciates their firmness,
one cannot condemn their severity.
To employ a person's firmness,
tolerate their severity.
Severity
is the mark of firmness.
Without severity, one cannot be firm.
If the gentle are not timid,
they cannot preserve their gentleness;
since one appreciates their gentleness,
one cannot condemn their timidity.
To employ a person's gentleness,
tolerate their timidity.
Timidity
is the mark of gentleness.
Without timidity, one cannot be gentle.
If the principled are not inflexible,
they cannot maintain their integrity;
