selecting people based on simplicity and forgiveness.
Some follow their words,
selecting people based on rhetoric and meaning.
Some verify their deeds,
selecting people based on results.
These eight methods are diverse and mixed,
each using what they consider acceptable as a standard,
thus杂乱无章.
Therefore, what they gain is little,
and what they lose is much.
They only take those similar to themselves,
and lose those different from themselves,
since they themselves are not comprehensive,
hence the losses are many.
Thus, there must be errors in hastily judging by appearance,
such as selecting by looks but finding actions contrary.
There are also mistakes in assessing changes in behavior,
like one who is physically in the rivers and lakes,
but mentally at the imperial court.
Therefore, in interacting and observing people,
following actions and trusting names,
they lose the true essence.
Thus, the sage listens to words and observes actions,
and if there is praise,
it must be tested.
So superficial talents that are overtly displayed
are considered extraordinary;
shallow wisdom easily seen,
appears remarkably fine.
Deep understanding that is silent
is considered empty;
profound wisdom internally bright,
appears insubstantial.
Analyzing subtle principles
is seen as keen insight;
delving into profound truths,
appears as sharp perception.
Reciting classifications
is considered philosophical;
forcibly categorizing things,
appears reasonable.
Liking to discuss rights and wrongs
is seen as judgmental;
recklessly speaking of是非,
seems discerning of good and bad.
Talking about reputations
is considered evaluating character;
forcefully debating worth and folly,
seems knowledgeable about people.
Calmly discussing governance
is seen as understanding state affairs;
wildly commenting on current events,
seems aware of the body politic.
It is like hearing sounds of creatures,
naming them according to their noise.
If these seven cannot be discerned,
things are all named based on their actions,
like hearing a cat's sound and calling it a cat,
hearing a sparrow's sound and calling it a sparrow,
not knowing what these two creatures are truly called.
The world's confusion
is all of this kind.
Thus, in the state of Lǔ, those wearing Confucian robes,
everyone calls them Confucians,
but when standing and questioning them,
only one is genuine.
For names do not match reality,
using them is ineffective,
the Southern Winnowing Basket cannot be used to winnow,
the Northern Dipper cannot be used to ladle wine.
Therefore it is said:
names are advanced by the mouth,
but reality retreats through actions.
The crowd sees the form and names it,
thus using it without verification.
Those with genuine inner qualities,
their names do not match their reality,
yet using them is effective,
true wisdom lies within,
the crowd cannot see it,
thus they have no external fame but internal substance.
Therefore, names are dismissed by the crowd,
but reality is revealed through actions,
effectiveness established then names become clear.
This is a common error in hasty judgment.
Shallow wisdom has no end,
deep wisdom has no beginning,
so the masses' observation of things
often fails at the start.
Thus, one must wait for their settled behavior,
then recognize them.
Look at where they settle,
observe where they abide,
and then how can one not know?
Therefore, in residence,
observe what they are content with;
those content with the old
are sincere in benevolence.
In advancement,
observe what they recommend;
recommending firm and upright individuals
shows depth in righteousness.
In wealth,
observe whom they associate with;
associating with stern and strong ones
demonstrates understanding of rites.
In hardship,
observe what they do;
engaging in classical studies
shows diligence in wisdom.
In poverty,
observe what they take.
Taking only their share
reflects adherence to trustworthiness.
Only then can one discern worthiness or lack thereof.
Those who act thus are worthy,
those who do the opposite are not.
This is again through testing,
not initial appearance.
Knowing through testing,
how can it be mere physiognomy!
So knowing the substance
is not enough to know the strategy.
Strategy lies in adaptability,
not in constant standards.
Moreover, among all the people under heaven,
one cannot interact with everyone.
Thus, observing their external appearance
can yield some understanding,
but is insufficient for complete knowledge.
Some have changing aspirations,
transforming with circumstances;
thus Shìzǔ missed it with Péng Méng,
and Cáo Gōng missed it with Dǒng Zhuó.
Some have desires not yet fulfilled,
or change their minds after attainment;
Lǐ Yì initially devoted himself to Guāngwǔ,
but ultimately turned to Shènggōng.
Some strive hard in poverty,
others indulge desires upon success.
Wáng Mǎng initially lived as a commoner with humility,
but ended in extreme extravagance.
This is also a failure in assessing settled behavior.
With changes in disposition like this,
who can determine them?
From this, it is argued,
to grasp both essentials,
is the difficulty of knowing them is hard.
Knowing their true nature,
and discerning their changes,
thus it is not something ordinary people can scrutinize.
What is meant by the difficulty of having no means to demonstrate one's worth?
Those of superior talent remain unrecognized,
which is inherently hard to identify and know.
Some who are recognized are in their youth or lowly status,
and pass away before achieving prominence;
before they can be advanced and established,
the person has already been lost.
Some who are recognized
are not promoted before their demise;
before they can be selected and elevated,
they have already departed from the world.
Some are like a lofty tune with few who can join in,
their advocacy goes unappreciated;
Gōngshū Zuò recommended Shāng Yāng,
but the King of Wèi did not employ him.
Some are of humble status and weak influence,
their words are not heeded;
Qín Xī recommended Bǎilǐ Xī,
and his head and feet were shattered.
Some possess abilities not favored by the times,
and are not trusted or valued;
Empress Dòu favored Huáng-Lǎo teachings,
how could Confucian scholars gain advancement?
Some are not in the right position,
with no means to be selected;
Biàn Hé, not encountered by a craftsman,
thus wept holding his uncut jade.
Some are in their positions,
yet face constraints and pressures.
Hé Wǔ recommended Gōngsūn Lù,
but was opposed by the Wáng clan.
Thus, for a fine talent to be recognized as genuine,
it is not even one in ten thousand encounters.
Though the talent may be excellent,
it must meet a true appreciator.
Even if a true appreciator is met,
it must coincide with an enlightened ruler.
The convergence of these three conditions
is not even one in ten thousand meetings.
It requires recognition of the genuine and being in position,
truly not even one in a hundred exists.
Even if one's true worth is recognized,
one may not be in the right position.
To have the position and power to recommend effectively,
it should be not even ten in a hundred matches.
Recognition requires being in position,
and wisdom must also be appropriate.
Some have clarity enough to recognize the genuine,
but face obstacles and usurpation,
and are unwilling to recommend;
though able to distinguish worth from folly, they are constrained by hindrances,
hence some are unwilling.
Some are eager to recommend,
but cannot recognize the genuine.
Those in positions,
though well-intentioned toward the worthy,
lack the clarity to discern.
Therefore, the knowing and the unknowing
mingle chaotically in the general confusion.
Some favor the worthy but cannot recognize them,
others know the worthy but are envious at heart,
so employment and non-employment
are alike in the mass confusion,
tangled and disordered.
Those who truly know
suffer from being unable to achieve effectiveness;
without rank or position,
there is no way to demonstrate and achieve.
Those who do not know
also consider themselves unacquainted.
Though in position,
they cannot recognize.
This is what is called the difficulty of having no means to demonstrate one's worth.
Hence it is said there are two difficulties in the effectiveness of knowing people.
Therefore, the ruler should always exercise his intelligence and wisdom,
broaden his vision and hearing,
openly promote those in obscurity,
extensively seek the talented and virtuous,
recommend the capable without avoiding enemies,
select the worthy without neglecting the hidden,
only then can the state be governed,
and achievements can be accomplished.
Chapter Twelve: Resolving Disputes
The virtuous and good do not boast of their merits,
let alone over trivial matters.
Relinquish anger and abandon contention,
and you shall surely bear glory and blessings.
Chapter Twelve: On Resolving Disputes
For goodness, taking non-boasting as greatness,
doing good yet boasting of one's ability,
is belittled by the multitude.
For worthiness, self-conceit brings loss.
Practicing worthiness while eliminating the mindset of self-importance—
where would one go without gain?
Thus, Shùn yielded based on virtue,
and his righteousness became renowned;
Tāng humbled himself without delay,
and his sage-like reverence daily ascended;
though these two emperors were endowed with heavenly sage virtue,
born with superior wisdom,
they still embraced toil and humility,
hastening to step back and lower themselves,
only then did their trustworthiness and righteousness become known,
radiantly occupying the celestial throne.
Xì Zhì considered himself superior to others,
and suppressed subordinates excessively;
Wáng Shū loved contention,
and ended up fleeing.
These two great officers boasted of their achievements and looked down on others,
one saw his clan exterminated,
the other escaped disaster by fleeing.
From this perspective,
the ways of contention and yielding—
are they not vastly different?
Thus, humble yielding and lowering oneself
are the smooth path to flourishing advancement;
the reason rivers and seas are kings of all valleys
is because they dwell low.
Arrogant striving and encroachment
are perilous paths to ruin and obstruction.
The reason rhinoceroses and tigers fall into cages
is because of their fierce, predatory nature.
Therefore, the noble person in action dares not exceed proper standards,
in ambition dares not override established norms.
Feet do not step recklessly,
always mindful of stepping back and lowering.
Inwardly diligent for self-improvement,
outwardly humble and yielding with reverence and caution.
Alone, one dares not do wrong,
stepping out as if meeting an honored guest.
Thus, resentment and trouble do not touch one,
and glory and fortune extend long.
External harms do not injure,
descendants rely on this for safety.
Petty persons, however, are not so:
boasting of achievements and flaunting abilities,
fond of belittling others.
From the start, regardless of scale,
their hearts swell to dominate others.
Thus, those ahead are harmed by people;
boasting of ability and running wild—
this is what people resent.
Those with merit are slandered by people;
relying on merit and becoming arrogant—
this is what people defame.
Those who fail are gloated over by people.
When they collapse,
it is what people relish.
Thus, riding abreast and vying to lead,
they cannot surpass each other;
petty persons compete for advancement,
their wisdom unable to outdo,
racing together on dangerous paths,
trampling over one another.
Both wearied and broken,
overtaken by those behind.
Falling midway,
later ones ride over them,
like when hares die and hounds tire,
the farmer reaps the benefit.
From this, it is said,
the paths of contention and yielding—
their distinction is clear.
The noble person upholds yielding,
thus traversing ten thousand miles with a clear road;
the petty person loves contention,
feet unmoved yet the path blocked.
However, those who are fond of winning
still refuse to acknowledge this.
Greed leads to a competitive nature,
and even when exposed to the ethos of virtuous deference,
their minds remain clouded,
claiming that ancient people gained by yielding,
while modern people lose by yielding.
Convinced of their own rightness,
they rise to contend.
They consider being ahead as swift and sharp,
and staying behind as stagnation;
thus they rush anxiously in action and repose,
with no time to groom their chariots.
They view being among the masses as lowly submission,
and stepping over ranks as exceptional prowess;
if they can boast of surpassing others,
they feel no shame in overreaching their status.
They see yielding to rivals as disgraceful retreat,
and oppressing superiors as lofty valor.
Hence, Zhào Chuān disregarded the commander-in-chief,
and Zhìzǐ led his flank army to ruin.
Thus, resisting and charging forward,
they cannot turn back on their own.
It is like tigers and wolves devouring living creatures,
then developing a murderous fury.
When resistance meets virtue,
it must result in yielding and lowering oneself;
as when Lìn Xiàngrú yielded to Lián Pō,
both reaped benefits.
When resistance meets violence,
it inevitably provokes conflict and hardship;
as when Guàn Fū refused to defer to Tián Fén,
both incurred blame.
Once conflict arises,
the logic of right and wrong becomes muddled and hard to clarify;
both sides consider themselves right and the other wrong,
so who can clarify it?
Muddled and difficult to clarify,
how is it different from self-destruction?
When two tigers fight,
the smaller dies,
the larger is injured,
how can both remain intact?
Moreover, when people slander others,
it all stems from grievances and leads to conflicts;
if there were no underlying resentment,
even when incidents occur,
they wouldn't result in slander or harm.
They must latch onto events,
and embellish the details.
All slander and defamation
rely on incidents to be fabricated.
As for the listeners,
though not entirely convinced,
they still half believe it.
Because the words have a semblance of truth,
half of the listeners believe them.
One's own retaliation
is much the same.
When counter-slandering in return,
it adds wings and a tail to the conflict.
In the end,
each side is half-believed.
Belief spreads far and wide.
Both have their appearances,
but the truth is unknown,
so listeners near and far
are half convinced by one side,
and half by the other.
Thus, those who argue fiercely
are merely swapping insults to destroy themselves;
if you point out others' flaws,
others will point out your faults,
even if you insult others,
you bring insult upon yourself.
Those who compete in verbal disputes
are lending hands to beat themselves;
angry words lead to forceful contention,
if you strike others,
others will strike you back,
this is lending hands to beat oneself.
How utterly deluded and mistaken this is!
Lending hands to beat oneself,
lending mouths to insult oneself,
if not delusion, then what?
Yet tracing back to the origin,
has there ever been self-reflection and strict self-blame
that led to disputes and lawsuits?
If one can self-reflect,
others will too,
both refraining from contention,
how could disputes and lawsuits arise?
It all stems from insufficient inner forgiveness,
and unceasing external expectations.
The reason for contention
is the inability to forgive oneself and self-reflect internally,
while endlessly expecting from others externally.
Some resent others for belittling them,
some envy others for surpassing them.
Thus, the heart contends,
never ceasing.
If I am shallow and others belittle me,
then it is because I am flawed and they are upright;
being flawed and belittled
is only fitting.
If I am virtuous and others do not recognize it,
then being belittled is not my fault.
Being close yet harmed instead,
is only fitting.
If others are virtuous and ahead of me,
then my virtue is not yet sufficient;
their virtue is superior,
so it is only fitting.
If virtue is equal and they precede me,
then my virtue is slightly lesser in proximity;
with equal virtue and seniority in age,
it is only normal.
What is there to resent?
Moreover, when two virtuous individuals are indistinguishable,
the one who can yield is the outstanding one;
with equal talent and no contention over superiority,
the crowd praises their humility.
When contending for excellence is unresolved,
the one who uses force becomes the wearied;
if excellence is equal and fame undifferentiated,
the crowd despises their fighting.
Therefore, Lìn Xiàngrú won over Lián Pō by turning his chariot around,
and Kòu Xún earned respect from Jiǎ Fù by avoiding conflict.
These two virtuous individuals,
knowing the path of contention is not to be taken,
thus turned their chariots to retreat or welcomed with wine and roast meat,
so Lián and Jiǎ bared their arms in apology,
and the contention vanished.
The reversal of circumstances
is what the gentleman calls the Way.
Dragons and snakes hibernate to preserve themselves,
inchworms curl to extend later.
Insects are tiny creatures,
yet they know to coil and bend,
how much more should humans!
Therefore, the nobleman understands that bending can lead to stretching,
so he endures humiliation without refusal;
as when Hán Xìn stooped under the humiliation of crawling between another's legs.
He knows that humility and deference can overcome enemies,
thus he yields without hesitation.
This is what is meant by Zhǎn Xǐ feasting the Qí army.
When it reaches its ultimate point,
it turns calamity into blessing,
as when Jìn Wén retreated three stages from Chǔ,
and achieved the merit of Chéngpú.
Bending before an enemy can turn them into a friend,
as when Lián Pō was confronted by Lìn Xiàngrú,
and they became friends willing to die for each other.
Thus, enmity does not extend to descendants,
and a fine reputation spreads endlessly.
Descendants bear its glory and shelter,
and bamboo and silk record its lofty righteousness.
Is not the way of the nobleman
indeed vast?
If one is biased, impatient, and fond of contention,
then one's life is endangered in the present,
how can there be blessings for the future?
Moreover, the nobleman can endure slight and minor grievances,
thus avoiding major disputes that arise from conflict;
major disputes start from tiny seeds,
so the nobleman is cautious in small matters.
The petty person cannot bear small resentments,
and ultimately suffers glaring defeat and disgrace.
The petty person considers minor faults harmless and does not rid themselves of them,
so their crimes grow beyond remedy,
and their evils accumulate beyond salvation.
If resentment is slight and one yields to it,
it can still be considered a virtue of humility;
if resentment is minor,
then the virtue of humility can eliminate it.
If change is in its bud and one contends over it,
then disaster forms and cannot be saved.
A tiny stream flowing unceasingly
eventually becomes a river;
water leaking can overturn a boat,
how can it be saved?
Thus, Chén Yú, due to the change in Zhāng Ěr,
ultimately suffered the harm of separation and death;
thinking to avenge a momentary anger,
he forgot the lifelong evil,
so his body perished and his lineage ended.
Péng Chǒng, because of the rift with Zhū Fú,
finally met with the disaster of overthrow and ruin.
Resenting a minor issue of supervision and blame,
he violated the grand plan from start to finish,
so his clan was destroyed and his family extinguished.
The pivot of fortune and misfortune,
can one not be cautious?
Two women contended over mulberry trees,
and the calamity between Wú and Chǔ arose;
Jì and Hòu fought over roosters,
and the conflict in the state of Lǔ erupted.
Is it not fearsome?
Is it not fearsome?
Therefore, the noble person's pursuit of victory
takes yielding and deference as sharp weapons;
where yielding and deference go,
there are no formidable adversaries ahead.
With self-cultivation as a protective shield,
refining oneself through reverence,
nothing can harm them.
In stillness, they close the mysterious gate of silence and oblivion;
in action, they follow the path of respect and compliance.
When the time calls for stillness,
they shut tightly and remain mysteriously silent;
when the time calls for action,
they tread the right path before advancing.
Thus, victory is achieved without visible contention,
with movement and stillness perfectly timed,
so the victory has no one to compete with,
as contention does not rely on force,
hence the success of victory becomes evident.
The enemy submits without fostering resentment.
With weapons unused,
how could resentment arise?
In such a state, regret and resentment do not show in voice or expression,
so how could there be overt contention?
If even facial composure remains unmoved,
how much less would physical struggle occur?
Those who engage in overt contention
must consider themselves virtuous,
yet others see them as treacherous and biased.
Believing oneself to be virtuous,
stubbornly insisting on one's own views,
affirming oneself and negating others—
how can others not contend?
If one truly lacks treacherous virtue,
there is no basis for slander;
but if one is indeed treacherous,
how can there be any point in disputing with them?
To dispute with someone treacherous
is like caging a rhinoceros or provoking a tiger—
is that advisable?
Their anger harming others
is inevitable.
The "Yì Jīng" says:
"Those who are treacherous and act contrary,
invite disputes."
"Disputes inevitably gather a crowd."
With treacherous words and contrary actions,
they will surely stir up others and lead to disputes.
"Lǎo Zǐ" says:
"It is precisely because they do not contend
that no one in the world can contend with them."
Those who prioritize humility and deference
encounter no contention wherever they go.
Therefore, the noble person recognizes that the path of contention is not to be taken.
Those who tread the path of contention
are bound to overturn their cart and bring disaster upon themselves.
Thus, transcending common customs and ascending to the heights,
one stands alone above the three grades.
What are the three grades?
Having no merit yet boasting of oneself,
is the first grade;
empty and self-praising,
thus it is the lowest grade.
Having merit and flaunting it,
is the second grade;
boasting of one's abilities,
thus it is the middle grade.
Having great merit yet not boasting,
is the third grade.
Attributing the merit to others,
thus it is the highest grade.
Foolish yet fond of winning,
is the first grade;
not measuring one's own capacity,
thus it is the lowest grade.
Worthy yet exalting oneself over others,
is the second grade;
praising one's own abilities,
thus it is the middle grade.
Worthy and able to yield,
is the third grade.
Returning goodness to others,
thus it is the highest grade.
Lenient with oneself but strict with others,
is the first grade;
by nature unforgiving toward others,
thus it is the lowest grade.
Strict with oneself and strict with others,
is the second grade;
narrow-minded and harsh,
thus it is the middle grade.
Strict with oneself but lenient with others,
is the third grade.
Disciplining oneself and forgiving others,
thus it is the highest grade.
All these instances,
are wonders of the Way,
variations in phenomena.
The mind not purely unified,
this is what is called wondrous variation.
Only after three transformations can one attain it,
thus none can match it.
Petty men remain in their lowest grade,
how could they ever reach it!
Only those who understand the Way and grasp transformation,
can then abide in it.
Abiding in the highest grade without losing it.
Therefore, Mèng Zhīfǎn, by not boasting,
gained the sage's praise;
not flaunting his merit,
fine reputation naturally arose.
Guǎn Shū, by declining rewards,
received generous and weighty gifts.
Not coveting the reward,
fine gifts came of themselves.
How could this be achieved through deceitful means?
It was the natural union of pure virtue.
Was it intentional—not boasting, declining rewards, feigning emotion to seek fame?
Rather, it was utmost sincerity arising from within,
naturally aligning with principle.
The noble man knows that self-diminishment brings benefit,
thus with one achievement, he gains twofold praise;
through self-diminishment, his conduct is perfected and his name established.
The petty man does not know that self-aggrandizement brings harm,
thus with one boast, he loses both;
through self-praise, his conduct is ruined and his name lost.
From this, it can be said:
those who do not boast,
are the ones who truly achieve;
those who do not contend,
are the ones who truly win.
Not boasting, yet their fame shines;
not contending, yet principle is attained.
Yielding to opponents,
is how one conquers them;
humbling oneself before the multitude,
is how one rises above them.
Retreating and yielding, yet the enemy submits;
modest and respectful, yet virtue shines.
If the noble man truly perceives the peril of contentious paths,
and alone rides high on the mysterious way,
then his radiance blazes forth, renewed daily,
and his virtuous reputation rivals the ancients.
Avoiding the dangerous road of wrath and excess,
roaming freely in the highest grade alone,
distancing himself from the chirping of sparrows,
matching the cry of the phoenix in the vast mystery,
then his virtuous light will shine unto the present and future,
his pure radiance equaling that of bygone eras.
